We deploy this tool to measure the intrinsic dimensionality of layers, showing in some cases needless over-parameterization; to probe learning dynamics throughout training, finding that networks converge to final representations from the bottom up; to show where class-specific information in networks is formed; and to suggest new training regimes that simultaneously save computation and overfit less. Code: https://github.com/google/svcca/

papers.title: How multilingual is Multilingual BERT?
papers.research_question: Why is Multilingual BERT (M-BERT) effective at zero-shot cross-lingual model transfer?
papers.core_contribution: M-BERT learns multilingual representations from monolingual corpora, enabling zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, but transfer effectiveness depends on typological similarity and script consistency.
papers.conclusion: M-BERT's cross-lingual transfer ability is due to multilingual representations learned from monolingual data, but for full effectiveness across all language pairs, explicit multilingual training objectives are needed.
papers.key_findings:
M-BERT can perform cross-lingual transfer even between languages with different scripts, indicating deep multilingual representations beyond vocabulary memorization.
Transfer performance is higher for typologically similar languages, suggesting that the model maps structures but does not learn systematic transformations for different word orders.
M-BERT generalizes to code-switched text when trained on monolingual data, showing its multilingual representation capability.
The model struggles with transliterated text, indicating limitations in handling non-standard scripts without explicit training.
The feature space of M-BERT allows for finding translation pairs through vector arithmetic, demonstrating a shared multilingual subspace.
papers.limitation:
Transfer is less accurate for languages with different word orders, such as English and Japanese.
M-BERT does not generalize well to transliterated text without explicit transliteration signals.
future_direction: Incorporate explicit multilingual training objectives to improve transfer to typologically divergent and transliterated targets.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we show that Multilingual BERT (M-BERT), released by Devlin et al. (2018) as a single language model pre-trained from monolingual corpora in 104 languages, is surprisingly good at zero-shot cross-lingual model transfer, in which task-specific annotations in one language are used to fine-tune the model for evaluation in another language. To understand why, we present a large number of probing experiments, showing that transfer is possible even to languages in different scripts, that transfer works best between typologically similar languages, that monolingual corpora can train models for code-switching, and that the model can find translation pairs. From these results, we can conclude that M-BERT does create multilingual representations, but that these representations exhibit systematic deficiencies affecting certain language pairs.

papers.title: Discovering Chunks in Neural Embeddings for Interpretability
papers.research_question: Can the cognitive mechanism of chunking be leveraged to interpret high-dimensional neural population activities in artificial neural networks? The paper tests the 'reflection hypothesis' that neural network activities reflect regularities in the data they are trained on.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a novel interpretability framework that uses the cognitive principle of chunking to identify recurring patterns (chunks) in neural embeddings, showing these chunks reflect data regularities and can causally influence model behavior.
papers.conclusion: The cognitive tendency for chunking can be leveraged to segment high-dimensional neural activity into recurring, interpretable chunks, revealing a structured reflection of the world within artificial neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
In simple RNNs trained on artificial sequences, hidden states reflect input regularities and can be extracted as interpretable chunks using discrete sequence chunking.
Extracted chunks in RNNs have a causal role: grafting these hidden states alters network predictions and can facilitate compositional learning.
In LLMs (LLaMA3-8B), neural population averaging can extract chunks corresponding to recurring words/concepts, with the extracted subpopulation activity serving as a classifier for the signal.
Unsupervised chunk discovery in LLM embeddings reveals chunks that correlate with abstract concepts like part-of-speech tags, suggesting they capture syntactic information.
The number and diversity of neural population chunks increase with the complexity and hierarchical structure of the input sequence, supporting the reflection hypothesis.
papers.limitation: The approach is an initial proof of concept and has limitations. Future work is needed to test it across different models, establish theoretical foundations, and refine chunk extraction methods.
future_direction: Test the reflection hypothesis across different models.
Establish theoretical foundations for the approach.
Refine chunk extraction methods, such as capturing multi-token chunks in unsupervised discovery.
Extend the framework toward nonparametric chunk discovery.
papers.abstract: Understanding neural networks is challenging due to their high-dimensional, interacting components. Inspired by human cognition, which processes complex sensory data by chunking it into recurring entities, we propose leveraging this principle to interpret artificial neural population activities. Biological and artificial intelligence share the challenge of learning from structured, naturalistic data, and we hypothesize that the cognitive mechanism of chunking can provide insights into artificial systems. We first demonstrate this concept in recurrent neural networks (RNNs) trained on artificial sequences with imposed regularities, observing that their hidden states reflect these patterns, which can be extracted as a dictionary of chunks that influence network responses. Extending this to large language models (LLMs) like LLaMA, we identify similar recurring embedding states corresponding to concepts in the input, with perturbations to these states activating or inhibiting the associated concepts. By exploring methods to extract dictionaries of identifiable chunks across neural embeddings of varying complexity, our findings introduce a new framework for interpreting neural networks, framing their population activity as structured reflections of the data they process.

papers.title: Distillation Dynamics: Towards Understanding Feature-Based Distillation in Vision Transformers
papers.research_question: Why does feature-based knowledge distillation, which works well for CNNs, fail when applied to Vision Transformers (ViTs), and what is the root cause of negative transfer?
papers.core_contribution: This paper reveals that ViTs exhibit a distinctive U-shaped information processing pattern (compression followed by expansion) and identifies a fundamental representational paradigm mismatch between teacher and student models as the root cause of negative transfer in feature-based distillation, providing essential theoretical guidance for designing effective ViT compression strategies.
papers.conclusion: Successful knowledge transfer in Vision Transformers requires moving beyond naive feature mimicry to methods that respect the fundamental representational constraints and the U-shaped information processing dynamics of these architectures.
papers.key_findings:
ViT models exhibit a learned U-shaped pattern in information entropy and activation magnitude across layers, indicating an initial compression phase followed by a task-specific expansion phase.
The failure of feature-based distillation in ViTs stems from a representational mismatch: teacher models employ distributed, high-dimensional encoding in later layers that smaller student models cannot replicate due to limited channel capacity.
Late-layer feature alignment actively harms student performance (negative transfer) because it forces the student to adopt a representational paradigm incompatible with its capacity, disrupting its natural learning progression.
Frequency spectrum analysis shows teacher ViTs transition from low-pass to uniform, high-energy spectra in late layers, while CNNs maintain low-pass spectra, explaining why feature mimicry works for CNNs but fails for ViTs.
The U-shaped information processing signature is a consistent learned behavior across different ViT architectures (e.g., CaiT, standard ViT) and training paradigms (supervised, self-supervised like MAE).
papers.abstract: While feature-based knowledge distillation has proven highly effective for compressing CNNs, these techniques unexpectedly fail when applied to Vision Transformers (ViTs), often performing worse than simple logit-based distillation. We provide the first comprehensive analysis of this phenomenon through a novel analytical framework termed as "distillation dynamics", combining frequency spectrum analysis, information entropy metrics, and activation magnitude tracking. Our investigation reveals that ViTs exhibit a distinctive U-shaped information processing pattern: initial compression followed by expansion. We identify the root cause of negative transfer in feature distillation: a fundamental representational paradigm mismatch between teacher and student models. Through frequency-domain analysis, we show that teacher models employ distributed, high-dimensional encoding strategies in later layers that smaller student models cannot replicate due to limited channel capacity. This mismatch causes late-layer feature alignment to actively harm student performance. Our findings reveal that successful knowledge transfer in ViTs requires moving beyond naive feature mimicry to methods that respect these fundamental representational constraints, providing essential theoretical guidance for designing effective ViTs compression strategies. All source code and experimental logs are provided at https://github.com/thy960112/Distillation-Dynamics.

papers.title: Towards Biologically Plausible Deep Learning
papers.research_question: How can credit assignment in deep networks be achieved in a biologically plausible way, avoiding the implausible aspects of backpropagation?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a biologically plausible learning mechanism for deep networks that interprets Spike-Timing-Dependent Plasticity (STDP) as stochastic gradient descent and uses a variational EM framework with target propagation for credit assignment without backpropagation.
papers.conclusion: The proposed approach addresses several biological implausibility issues of backpropagation and provides a promising direction for biologically plausible deep learning, with experimental validation on MNIST.
papers.key_findings:
STDP can be interpreted as stochastic gradient descent if neural dynamics push firing rates towards better objective function values.
The training procedure corresponds to variational EM with approximate inference, implemented by neural dynamics.
Targetprop (difference target propagation) can estimate gradients without backpropagation, enabling biologically plausible deep learning.
The method can learn a generative model that produces good samples on MNIST, with log-likelihood comparable to other models.
The variational EM updates with noise can be interpreted as training a denoising auto-encoder over both visible and latent variables, and iterating the associated Markov chain yields better samples.
papers.limitation:
The approach does not address the synchronization issue (the 5th implausible element of backpropagation).
More work is needed to connect in more detail with biology, including neural implementation using spikes and constraints on weight signs.
future_direction: Incorporate lateral connections to implement priors on joint distributions between nearby neurons.
Explore the replacement of MAP-based inference by MCMC-like inference with noise injection.
Apply the ideas to supervised learning and reinforcement learning.
papers.abstract: Neuroscientists have long criticised deep learning algorithms as incompatible with current knowledge of neurobiology. We explore more biologically plausible versions of deep representation learning, focusing here mostly on unsupervised learning but developing a learning mechanism that could account for supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning. The starting point is that the basic learning rule believed to govern synaptic weight updates (Spike-Timing-Dependent Plasticity) arises out of a simple update rule that makes a lot of sense from a machine learning point of view and can be interpreted as gradient descent on some objective function so long as the neuronal dynamics push firing rates towards better values of the objective function (be it supervised, unsupervised, or reward-driven). The second main idea is that this corresponds to a form of the variational EM algorithm, i.e., with approximate rather than exact posteriors, implemented by neural dynamics. Another contribution of this paper is that the gradients required for updating the hidden states in the above variational interpretation can be estimated using an approximation that only requires propagating activations forward and backward, with pairs of layers learning to form a denoising auto-encoder. Finally, we extend the theory about the probabilistic interpretation of auto-encoders to justify improved sampling schemes based on the generative interpretation of denoising auto-encoders, and we validate all these ideas on generative learning tasks.

papers.title: Disentangled Representations in Neural Models
papers.research_question: How can we learn disentangled representations in neural models that are interpretable, reusable, and performant, without sacrificing performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces methods (DC-IGN and CFN) for learning disentangled representations in graphics and computation, which are interpretable, reusable, and performant without catastrophic forgetting.
papers.conclusion: Disentangled representations are valuable for interpretability and reuse, and the proposed methods (DC-IGN and CFN) are effective in learning such representations in the domains of graphics and computation.
papers.key_findings:
DC-IGN can learn a disentangled graphics code for 3D faces and chairs, enabling novel view synthesis and re-rendering under different lighting and pose conditions.
CFN can disentangle computational tasks, factorize a multitask learning problem, and is practically immune to catastrophic forgetting.
Explicit disentanglement training is critical for novel-view reconstruction compared to entangled representations.
The decoder in DC-IGN can function as a 3D rendering engine, indicating a truly disentangled representation.
CFN achieves disentanglement with no performance penalty and with fewer parameters than a traditional feedforward network.
papers.limitation:
The current formulation of SGVB is restricted to continuous latent variables, but real-world scenes may require discrete distributions.
Scaling to more complex scenes may require deeper architectures.
The decoder network might be replaced by a domain-specific decoder for fine-grained model-based inference.
future_direction: Experiment with deeper architectures to handle more complex scenes and object categories.
Extend the model to handle discrete distributions or to a recurrent setting.
Use importance-weighted autoencoders to capture more complex probabilistic structure.
Replace the decoder with a domain-specific decoder for fine-grained inference.
Explore multi-step CFN for deeper computations and curricula.
Investigate non-differentiable functions in CFN and hierarchical computation.
Unify the two approaches for unsupervised inference of factors of variation in videos.
papers.abstract: Representation learning is the foundation for the recent success of neural network models. However, the distributed representations generated by neural networks are far from ideal. Due to their highly entangled nature, they are di cult to reuse and interpret, and they do a poor job of capturing the sparsity which is present in real- world transformations. In this paper, I describe methods for learning disentangled representations in the two domains of graphics and computation. These methods allow neural methods to learn representations which are easy to interpret and reuse, yet they incur little or no penalty to performance. In the Graphics section, I demonstrate the ability of these methods to infer the generating parameters of images and rerender those images under novel conditions. In the Computation section, I describe a model which is able to factorize a multitask learning problem into subtasks and which experiences no catastrophic forgetting. Together these techniques provide the tools to design a wide range of models that learn disentangled representations and better model the factors of variation in the real world.

papers.title: Synergistic information supports modality integration and flexible learning in neural networks solving multiple tasks
papers.research_question: How and why synergistic information emerges in cognitive systems, and how these informational states map onto artificial neural networks in various learning modes.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that redundant information is required for robustness to perturbations, while synergistic information supports the integration of multiple modalities and enables flexible and efficient learning in neural networks.
papers.conclusion: Synergistic information is crucial for general-purpose learning as it supports integration of multiple modalities and flexible learning, while redundant information provides robustness.
papers.key_findings:
Synergy increases as neural networks learn multiple diverse tasks.
Performance in tasks requiring integration of multiple information sources critically relies on synergistic neurons.
Dropout increases network redundancy, corresponding to an increase in robustness.
Synergy is specifically linked to the integration of multiple modalities and flexible learning.
Redundant information provides robustness but is less efficient.
future_direction: Future work may seek to disentangle the relevance of each potential cause driving the importance of synergistic neurons.
Empirical evaluation of the conjectures about unique information in specialized circuits is an interesting avenue.
papers.abstract: Striking progress has recently been made in understanding human cognition by analyzing how its neuronal underpinnings are engaged in different modes of information processing. Specifically, neural information can be decomposed into synergistic, redundant, and unique features, with synergistic components being particularly aligned with complex cognition. However, two fundamental questions remain unanswered: (a) precisely how and why a cognitive system can become highly synergistic; and (b) how these informational states map onto artificial neural networks in various learning modes. To address these questions, here we employ an information-decomposition framework to investigate the information processing strategies adopted by simple artificial neural networks performing a variety of cognitive tasks in both supervised and reinforcement learning settings. Our results show that synergy increases as neural networks learn multiple diverse tasks. Furthermore, performance in tasks requiring integration of multiple information sources critically relies on synergistic neurons. Finally, randomly turning off neurons during training through dropout increases network redundancy, corresponding to an increase in robustness. Overall, our results suggest that while redundant information is required for robustness to perturbations in the learning process, synergistic information is used to combine information from multiple modalities -- and more generally for flexible and efficient learning. These findings open the door to new ways of investigating how and why learning systems employ specific information-processing strategies, and support the principle that the capacity for general-purpose learning critically relies in the system's information dynamics.

papers.title: Open Sesame: Getting inside BERT’s Linguistic Knowledge
papers.research_question: How and to what extent does BERT encode syntactically-sensitive hierarchical information or positionally-sensitive linear information?
papers.core_contribution: BERT encodes positional information in lower layers and switches to a hierarchically-oriented encoding on higher layers. The paper also introduces a 'confusion score' to quantify intrusion effects in BERT's self-attention mechanism.
papers.conclusion: BERT composes increasingly abstract hierarchical representations of linguistic structure using self-attention, but does not show the sharp sensitivity to hierarchical structure found in human processing.
papers.key_findings:
Diagnostic classifiers show BERT's lower layers encode positional information well, while higher layers encode hierarchical information.
The proposed confusion score reveals BERT's attention is sensitive to syntactic structure and grammatical features (number, gender) in subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora.
BERT's attention is not perfectly syntactic; it sometimes attends to grammatically inaccessible or mismatched distractors.
Confusion scores decrease with layer depth, and there is an increase in confusion at layer 4, coinciding with the degradation of positional information.
BERT's performance on possessive constructions in the subject noun task is poor, possibly due to ambiguity of the 's token.
papers.limitation:
BERT performed poorly on possessive constructions in the subject noun task, possibly due to ambiguity of the 's token.
BERT's attention is only incompletely modulated by structural and featural properties, and attention is sometimes spread across grammatically irrelevant elements.
future_direction: Investigate or visualize layer-on-layer changes in BERT’s structural and positional information, particularly between layers 3 and 4.
Retrieve the increasingly hierarchical representations of BERT across layers via the self-attention mechanism.
papers.abstract: How and to what extent does BERT encode syntactically-sensitive hierarchical information or positionally-sensitive linear information? Recent work has shown that contextual representations like BERT perform well on tasks that require sensitivity to linguistic structure. We present here two studies which aim to provide a better understanding of the nature of BERT's representations. The first of these focuses on the identification of structurally-defined elements using diagnostic classifiers, while the second explores BERT's representation of subject-verb agreement and anaphor-antecedent dependencies through a quantitative assessment of self-attention vectors. In both cases, we find that BERT encodes positional information about word tokens well on its lower layers, but switches to a hierarchically-oriented encoding on higher layers. We conclude then that BERT's representations do indeed model linguistically relevant aspects of hierarchical structure, though they do not appear to show the sharp sensitivity to hierarchical structure that is found in human processing of reflexive anaphora.

papers.title: Coloring the Black Box: Visualizing neural network behavior with a self-introspective model
papers.research_question: How can autoencoding the hidden activations of a neural network provide insight into its structure, behavior, and vulnerabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method called self-introspection, which uses an autoencoder to create a low-dimensional visualization of a neural network's hidden activations, enabling model evaluation, error estimation, layer reordering, and analysis of noise and adversarial attacks.
papers.conclusion: Self-introspection via autoencoders provides a flexible, interactive way to visualize and understand neural network behavior, offering potential for model evaluation, reliability assessment, and further research into interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Hidden activations of a trained model cluster by category in a low-dimensional embedding, with misclassifications occurring in fringe areas between clusters.
The method allows for real-time model evaluation and error estimation based on the activation patterns.
The hidden layers of a network can be reordered by their relevance to specific output categories, revealing a latent structure.
The activation space visualization can be used to study the network's response to input noise and adversarial attacks, showing trajectories from correct to incorrect classifications.
Error estimates from the self-introspective framework are higher for misclassified samples, suggesting its use as a confidence metric.
papers.limitation: The method is demonstrated on feedforward and convolutional networks with relatively simple datasets; its application to recurrent, convolutional, and attention-based models is noted as potential but not shown.
future_direction: Extending the method to recurrent, convolutional, and attention-based models.
Studying the reliability and structure of the low-dimensional representations for more complex problems.
Using the method for adversarial attack detection and as a human interface for model reliability in ensembles.
papers.abstract: The following work presents how autoencoding all the possible hidden activations of a network for a given problem can provide insight about its structure, behavior, and vulnerabilities. The method, termed self-introspection, can show that a trained model showcases similar activation patterns (albeit randomly distributed due to initialization) when shown data belonging to the same category, and classification errors occur in fringe areas where the activations are not as clearly defined, suggesting some form of random, slowly varying, implicit encoding occurring within deep networks, that can be observed with this representation. Additionally, obtaining a low-dimensional representation of all the activations allows for (1) real-time model evaluation in the context of a multiclass classification problem, (2) the rearrangement of all hidden layers by their relevance in obtaining a specific output, and (3) the obtainment of a framework where studying possible counter-measures to noise and adversarial attacks is possible. Self-introspection can show how damaged input data can modify the hidden activations, producing an erroneous response. A few illustrative are implemented for feedforward and convolutional models and the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets, showcasing its capabilities as a model evaluation framework.

papers.title: SVCCA: Singular Vector Canonical Correlation Analysis for Deep Learning\n Dynamics and Interpretability
papers.research_question: What is the intrinsic dimensionality of neural network layers and how do learning dynamics progress during training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SVCCA, a method for comparing neural network representations that is invariant to affine transforms, and uses it to show that layers have lower intrinsic dimensionality than the number of neurons, and that networks converge from the bottom up during training.
papers.conclusion: SVCCA is a powerful method for comparing neural network representations, providing insights into learning dynamics, intrinsic dimensionality, and enabling applications like model compression and improved training regimes.
papers.key_findings:
The intrinsic dimensionality of a layer is less than the number of neurons, and projecting onto the top SVCCA directions preserves accuracy without retraining.
Networks converge from the bottom up during training, with lower layers solidifying their representations earlier than higher layers.
SVCCA captures semantic class information, with similar classes having similar sensitivities in the network.
Freeze Training, based on the bottom-up convergence, can save computation and improve generalization by sequentially freezing lower layers during training.
SVCCA can be used for model compression by projecting layer outputs onto top SVCCA directions, reducing parameter count and computational cost.
papers.abstract:
We propose a new technique, Singular Vector Canonical Correlation Analysis
(SVCCA), a tool for quickly comparing two representations in a way that is both
invariant to affine transform (allowing comparison between different layers and
networks) and fast to compute (allowing more comparisons to be calculated than
with previous methods). We deploy this tool to measure the intrinsic
dimensionality of layers, showing in some cases needless over-parameterization;
to probe learning dynamics throughout training, finding that networks converge
to final representations from the bottom up; to show where class-specific
information in networks is formed; and to suggest new training regimes that
simultaneously save computation and overfit less. Code:
https://github.com/google/svcca/

papers.title: Identifying and Controlling Important Neurons in Neural Machine\n Translation
papers.research_question: How important are individual neurons for obtaining high-quality translations? Do individual neurons in NMT models contain interpretable linguistic information? Can we control MT output by intervening in the representation at the individual neuron level?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops unsupervised methods (based on correlations between models) for discovering important neurons in Neural Machine Translation models, shows these neurons impact translation quality and capture linguistic phenomena, and demonstrates how to control translations by modifying their activations.
papers.conclusion: The work indicates that not all information is distributed in NMT models, and that many human-interpretable grammatical and structural properties are captured by individual neurons. Moreover, modifying the activations of individual neurons allows controlling the translation output according to specified linguistic properties.
papers.key_findings:
Unsupervised correlation methods (MaxCorr, MinCorr, LinReg, SVCCA) can rank neurons by importance, with top-ranked neurons having a larger impact on translation quality when erased.
Many top-ranked neurons capture interpretable linguistic properties such as position in sentence, parentheses, tense, number, gender, and noun phrase segmentation.
Modifying the activations of individual neurons (e.g., tense neurons) allows for controlling translation output (e.g., changing verb tense) with varying degrees of success.
Different ranking methods highlight different types of information: MaxCorr and MinCorr tend to find position information, while LinReg and SVCCA find information distributed across tokens.
The work indicates that not all linguistic information in NMT models is fully distributed; some properties are captured by individual neurons.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to other NMT components (e.g., the decoder) and architectures (e.g., Transformer, convolutional seq2seq).
Develop more sophisticated ways to control translation output, for example by modifying representations in variational NMT architectures.
Apply the methods to other tasks beyond machine translation.
papers.abstract:
Neural machine translation (NMT) models learn representations containing
substantial linguistic information. However, it is not clear if such
information is fully distributed or if some of it can be attributed to
individual neurons. We develop unsupervised methods for discovering important
neurons in NMT models. Our methods rely on the intuition that different models
learn similar properties, and do not require any costly external supervision.
We show experimentally that translation quality depends on the discovered
neurons, and find that many of them capture common linguistic phenomena.
Finally, we show how to control NMT translations in predictable ways, by
modifying activations of individual neurons.

papers.title: Do Vision Transformers See Like Convolutional Neural Networks?
papers.research_question: How are Vision Transformers solving image tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds key representational differences between Vision Transformers (ViTs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), showing ViTs have more uniform layer representations, incorporate global information earlier via self-attention, and have stronger skip connections that propagate features differently.
papers.conclusion: ViTs and CNNs have clear differences in features and internal structure, with ViTs using global features early and strong skip connections, while local information aggregation is learned from scratch at scale. ViTs show strong spatial localization, promising for future uses like object detection.
papers.key_findings:
ViTs have a more uniform internal representation structure with greater similarity between lower and higher layers compared to the staged similarity in ResNets.
ViTs incorporate global information in lower layers through self-attention, while CNNs are restricted to local receptive fields; this leads to quantitatively different features.
Skip connections in ViTs are more influential than in ResNets, with a phase transition: early layers strongly propagate the CLS token, while later layers propagate spatial token representations.
ViTs preserve input spatial information more faithfully than ResNets in higher layers, especially when trained with a CLS token rather than global average pooling.
Large-scale pretraining data is crucial for ViTs to learn to attend locally in early layers and to develop high-quality intermediate representations for transfer learning.
papers.limitation: The study uses CKA, which summarizes measurements into a single scalar; while complemented with interventional tests and linear probes, more fine-grained methods may reveal additional insights.
papers.abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have so far been the de-facto model for visual data. Recent work has shown that (Vision) Transformer models (ViT) can achieve comparable or even superior performance on image classification tasks. This raises a central question: how are Vision Transformers solving these tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations? Analyzing the internal representation structure of ViTs and CNNs on image classification benchmarks, we find striking differences between the two architectures, such as ViT having more uniform representations across all layers. We explore how these differences arise, finding crucial roles played by self-attention, which enables early aggregation of global information, and ViT residual connections, which strongly propagate features from lower to higher layers. We study the ramifications for spatial localization, demonstrating ViTs successfully preserve input spatial information, with noticeable effects from different classification methods. Finally, we study the effect of (pretraining) dataset scale on intermediate features and transfer learning, and conclude with a discussion on connections to new architectures such as the MLP-Mixer.

papers.title: Subliminal Effects in Your Data: A General Mechanism via Log-Linearity
papers.research_question: Is there a general mechanism behind a broad suite of subliminal effects in language model training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Logit-Linear Selection (LLS), a method to select subsets of preference data that subliminally transfer behaviors, and provides a theoretical framework based on log-linearity to explain the phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: LLS provides a general mechanism for subliminal effects in language models, grounded in the log-linear structure of language models, with implications for data selection and safety.
papers.key_findings:
LLS can select subsets of real-world datasets to elicit hidden effects such as specific preferences, responding in a different language, and adopting a persona.
The subliminal effect persists across models with varying architectures, demonstrating universality.
The mechanism is explained by the log-linear abstraction and linear representations of language models.
Subliminal learning can occur even when the dataset contains no obvious instances of the target behavior.
The method works with preference data and can transfer behaviors across teacher-student model pairs, though more effectively when models are the same.
papers.limitation: The subliminal effect is weaker when the teacher and student models are different, and the reasons for this variation are not fully understood.
future_direction: Understanding the factors that account for variations in subliminal learning across different student models.
Developing defenses against subliminal learning in datasets.
Applying LLS for jailbreaking closed models and watermarking datasets.
papers.abstract: Training modern large language models (LLMs) has become a veritable smorgasbord of algorithms and datasets designed to elicit particular behaviors, making it critical to develop techniques to understand the effects of datasets on the model's properties. This is exacerbated by recent experiments that show datasets can transmit signals that are not directly observable from individual datapoints, posing a conceptual challenge for dataset-centric understandings of LLM training and suggesting a missing fundamental account of such phenomena. Towards understanding such effects, inspired by recent work on the linear structure of LLMs, we uncover a general mechanism through which hidden subtexts can arise in generic datasets. We introduce Logit-Linear-Selection (LLS), a method that prescribes how to select subsets of a generic preference dataset to elicit a wide range of hidden effects. We apply LLS to discover subsets of real-world datasets so that models trained on them exhibit behaviors ranging from having specific preferences, to responding to prompts in a different language not present in the dataset, to taking on a different persona. Crucially, the effect persists for the selected subset, across models with varying architectures, supporting its generality and universality.

papers.title: Learning and Understanding a Disentangled Feature Representation for Hidden Parameters in Reinforcement Learning
papers.research_question: How to learn a feature space that represents trajectories by their hidden parameter values in an unsupervised manner, and how to use this to analyze the effects of hidden parameters.
papers.core_contribution: Presents an unsupervised method to learn a disentangled feature representation for hidden parameters in RL, using a time-invariant RNN memory training algorithm and a latent bisimulation metric learning approach.
papers.conclusion: The approach successfully learns a feature representation for hidden parameters and demonstrates its utility in estimation and visualization, with potential for future extensions to more complex environments.
papers.key_findings:
The time-invariant RNN memory and latent bisimulation metric features outperform baseline world model features in hidden parameter estimation.
The learned feature space can be visualized to show clear separation by hidden parameter values.
The method can identify which state variables are most affected by hidden parameters by comparing stateful and non-stateful world models.
The world model can generate imagined trajectories for different hidden parameter values to visualize their effects.
papers.limitation:
The environments tested represent only a small subset of real-world challenges.
The method focuses on single discrete hidden parameters and does not handle multiple or continuous hidden parameters or dynamic latent variables.
future_direction: Estimating the number of hidden parameters in an environment and decoupling their individual effects.
Extending from static hidden parameters to dynamic latent variables that change at different time-scales.
Finding more effective ways to communicate hidden parameter information to human users.
papers.abstract: Hidden parameters are latent variables in reinforcement learning (RL) environments that are constant over the course of a trajectory. Understanding what, if any, hidden parameters affect a particular environment can aid both the development and appropriate usage of RL systems. We present an unsupervised method to map RL trajectories into a feature space where distance represents the relative difference in system behavior due to hidden parameters. Our approach disentangles the effects of hidden parameters by leveraging a recurrent neural network (RNN) world model as used in model-based RL. First, we alter the standard world model training algorithm to isolate the hidden parameter information in the world model memory. Then, we use a metric learning approach to map the RNN memory into a space with a distance metric approximating a bisimulation metric with respect to the hidden parameters. The resulting disentangled feature space can be used to meaningfully relate trajectories to each other and analyze the hidden parameter. We demonstrate our approach on four hidden parameters across three RL environments. Finally we present two methods to help identify and understand the effects of hidden parameters on systems.

papers.title: Language Models Represent Space and Time
papers.research_question: Do large language models learn coherent linear representations of space and time, i.e., do they form a world model?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models learn linear representations of space and time that are robust to prompting and unified across entity types, and individual 'space' and 'time' neurons exist that encode these coordinates.
papers.conclusion: Modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can recover spatial and temporal coordinates from internal activations, with performance increasing with model size and plateauing in middle layers.
Spatial and temporal features are linearly represented, as nonlinear probes do not improve performance.
Representations are robust to variations in prompting, though random tokens or capitalization degrade performance.
Probes generalize across entity types and to held-out geographic or temporal blocks, indicating unified representations.
Individual neurons exist that are highly predictive of space and time, and causal interventions confirm their importance.
papers.limitation:
Data comes only from English Wikipedia, skewing towards the Anglosphere, and entity type distribution is not uniform.
The true extent and structure of spatial and temporal representations remain unclear.
future_direction: Extracting representations in the model’s coordinate system rather than human coordinates, e.g., with sparse autoencoders.
Studying how these spatiotemporal representations are learned, recalled, and used internally across training checkpoints.
Investigating potential parallels with biological place and grid cells in the brain.
papers.abstract: The capabilities of large language models (LLMs) have sparked debate over whether such systems just learn an enormous collection of superficial statistics or a set of more coherent and grounded representations that reflect the real world. We find evidence for the latter by analyzing the learned representations of three spatial datasets (world, US, NYC places) and three temporal datasets (historical figures, artworks, news headlines) in the Llama-2 family of models. We discover that LLMs learn linear representations of space and time across multiple scales. These representations are robust to prompting variations and unified across different entity types (e.g. cities and landmarks). In addition, we identify individual "space neurons" and "time neurons" that reliably encode spatial and temporal coordinates. While further investigation is needed, our results suggest modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.

papers.title: Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT
papers.research_question: How are factual associations stored and recalled in autoregressive transformer language models, and can they be directly edited?
papers.core_contribution: Factual associations in GPT are stored in mid-layer feed-forward modules and can be directly edited using a rank-one update method (ROME), which achieves strong generalization and specificity.
papers.conclusion: Factual associations in autoregressive transformers are stored in mid-layer MLP modules and can be directly edited via localized weight updates, with ROME providing an effective method for such edits.
papers.key_findings:
Causal tracing reveals that mid-layer MLP modules at the last subject token are decisive for factual predictions.
The Rank-One Model Editing (ROME) method can effectively edit factual associations by updating a single MLP layer with a rank-one weight update.
ROME achieves strong generalization and specificity on counterfactual edits, outperforming previous fine-tuning and hypernetwork-based methods.
The early site (mid-layer MLP) and late site (late-layer attention) play different roles: MLP stores the association, and attention copies it to the output.
The paper introduces a new dataset, COUNTERFACT, for evaluating counterfactual model edits.
papers.limitation: Human evaluation reveals a reduction in fluency of generated text under ROME, which the automatic entropy measure does not capture.
papers.abstract: We analyze the storage and recall of factual associations in autoregressive transformer language models, finding evidence that these associations correspond to localized, directly-editable computations. We first develop a causal intervention for identifying neuron activations that are decisive in a model's factual predictions. This reveals a distinct set of steps in middle-layer feed-forward modules that mediate factual predictions while processing subject tokens. To test our hypothesis that these computations correspond to factual association recall, we modify feed-forward weights to update specific factual associations using Rank-One Model Editing (ROME). We find that ROME is effective on a standard zero-shot relation extraction (zsRE) model-editing task, comparable to existing methods. To perform a more sensitive evaluation, we also evaluate ROME on a new dataset of counterfactual assertions, on which it simultaneously maintains both specificity and generalization, whereas other methods sacrifice one or another. Our results confirm an important role for mid-layer feed-forward modules in storing factual associations and suggest that direct manipulation of computational mechanisms may be a feasible approach for model editing. The code, dataset, visualizations, and an interactive demo notebook are available at https://rome.baulab.info/

papers.title: BIRD: Behavior Induction via Representation-structure Distillation
papers.research_question: Can aligned behavior be transferred even when the teacher and student differ in architecture, task, and training data?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces BIRD, a framework for transferring aligned behavior by distilling the structure of a teacher's internal representations into a student, without requiring shared data or tasks, and shows that transfer success is predictable by teacher representation properties.
papers.conclusion: BIRD provides a flexible, data-free mechanism for transferring aligned behavior across models and domains, advancing weak-to-strong generalization and enabling scalable, reusable alignment.
papers.key_findings:
BIRD outperforms fine-tuning, transfer learning, and continual learning methods in transferring out-of-distribution robustness, improving robust accuracy by up to 16% over the strongest baseline.
BIRD remains effective even when the teacher is trained on a much simpler dataset and is 25× smaller than the student.
Three interpretable properties of the teacher’s representation space (task relevance, behavioral relevance, and complementary knowledge) explain up to 85% of the variance in transfer success.
BIRD can improve weak-to-strong generalization in NLP when combined with soft-label distillation, though the effect is not universal.
Transfer success is predictable and actionable, offering practical guidance for teacher and layer selection.
papers.limitation:
Core analyses focus on robustness in vision, with only preliminary results in NLP.
Transfer success is likely bounded by the student’s capacity and task complexity.
Currently supervise alignment at a single layer; multi-layer or hierarchical extensions may be needed.
Effectiveness depends on the teacher; if the teacher encodes misaligned behaviors, BIRD may transfer them.
future_direction: Extending BIRD to other behaviors (e.g., honesty) and modalities (e.g., multimodal reasoning).
Quantifying the saturation effect of transfer success more precisely.
Exploring multi-layer or hierarchical extensions to capture deeper structural alignment.
papers.abstract: Human-aligned deep learning models exhibit behaviors consistent with human values, such as robustness, fairness, and honesty. Transferring these behavioral properties to models trained on different tasks or data distributions remains challenging: aligned behavior is easily forgotten during fine-tuning, and collecting task-specific data that preserves this behavior can be prohibitively costly. We introduce BIRD (Behavior Induction via Representation-structure Distillation), a flexible framework for transferring aligned behavior by matching the internal representation structure of a student model to that of a teacher. Applied to out-of-distribution robustness in image classification, BIRD outperforms fine-tuning, transfer learning, and continual learning methods, improving robust accuracy by up to 16% over the next strongest baseline. It remains effective even when the teacher is trained on a much simpler dataset and is $25 \times$ smaller than the student. In a large-scale study of over 400 teacher-student pairs, we show that three interpretable and computable properties of the teacher's representations (i.e., task relevance, behavioral relevance, and complementary knowledge) explain up to 85% of the variance in transfer success. These insights offer practical guidance for teacher selection and design. BIRD turns small, well-aligned models into scalable alignment seeds, removing a key bottleneck in deploying safe AI systems in the wild.

papers.title: Understanding Interpretability by generalized distillation in Supervised Classification
papers.research_question: How can interpretability be defined and quantified from an information-theoretic perspective, decoupled from human understanding, using a distillation-like framework?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an information-theoretic framework for interpretability based on distillation, decoupling interpretability from human understanding and providing theoretical bounds for Piece-Wise Linear Neural Networks.
papers.conclusion: The interpretation-by-distillation framework provides a novel interpretability definition from an information-theoretic perspective, with theoretical bounds for ReLU networks, and demonstrates stability and conformity to human understanding.
papers.key_findings:
The interpretability measure conforms to human understanding when explaining predictions of InceptionV3 on Stanford40, with higher interpretability when cropped images contain relevant objects.
Ensembles of simpler models (e.g., SVM, Decision Tree, Logistic Regression) can interpret complex models like MiniVGGNet with high interpretability.
Interpretability converges as the number of query points increases, demonstrating stability of the empirical interpretation.
The interpretability formulation is decoupled from accuracy, as shown by Decision Tree having higher accuracy but lower interpretability on MNIST compared to Fashion-MNIST.
The framework exhibits double ascent behavior in interpretability, aligning with modern deep learning phenomena.
papers.limitation:
Theoretical interpretability estimates are far from empirical estimates due to exponential complexity bounds.
Model entropy definition only considers arrangement of decision boundary, not shape.
Theoretical bounds are limited to Piece-Wise Linear Networks (PWLNs).
future_direction: Explore the effect of dataset complexity on interpretability.
Incorporate the shape of the decision boundary into the entropy definition.
Extend the theoretical bounds to other networks like CNNs when their complexities are defined.
papers.abstract: The ability to interpret decisions taken by Machine Learning (ML) models is fundamental to encourage trust and reliability in different practical applications. Recent interpretation strategies focus on human understanding of the underlying decision mechanisms of the complex ML models. However, these strategies are restricted by the subjective biases of humans. To dissociate from such human biases, we propose an interpretation-by-distillation formulation that is defined relative to other ML models. We generalize the distillation technique for quantifying interpretability, using an information-theoretic perspective, removing the role of ground-truth from the definition of interpretability. Our work defines the entropy of supervised classification models, providing bounds on the entropy of Piece-Wise Linear Neural Networks (PWLNs), along with the first theoretical bounds on the interpretability of PWLNs. We evaluate our proposed framework on the MNIST, Fashion-MNIST and Stanford40 datasets and demonstrate the applicability of the proposed theoretical framework in different supervised classification scenarios.

papers.title: From superposition to sparse codes: interpretable representations in neural networks
papers.research_question: How can we relate distributed neural representations back to human-interpretable concepts?
papers.core_contribution: This perspective paper presents a theoretical framework explaining how neural networks encode information in superposition and argues that sparse coding, supported by identifiability theory and compressed sensing, can extract interpretable, sparse features from these distributed representations.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that neural networks learn linear representations of latent variables and that sparse coding can recover interpretable features, providing a foundation for understanding neural representations in both artificial and biological systems.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks encode information in superposition, meaning multiple concepts are linearly combined in a shared representational space.
Identifiability theory shows that neural networks trained for classification recover latent features up to a linear transformation.
Sparse coding methods, such as sparse autoencoders, can extract disentangled, interpretable features from superposed neural representations.
Quantitative interpretability metrics, like psychophysics tasks, are needed to assess the success of feature extraction methods.
The framework bridges insights from theoretical neuroscience, representation learning, and interpretability research.
papers.limitation:
The framework assumes sparse latent variables in Euclidean space, whereas some latent variables (e.g., object pose) may have non-Euclidean topology, and the linear representation hypothesis may only hold approximately in such cases.
Practical recovery of sparse codes in large-scale models remains challenging, requiring more efficient and scalable sparse coding algorithms.
Interpretability scores based on pairwise human similarity judgments are insufficient as they depend on context, motivating the need for contextualized similarity metrics.
future_direction: Extending the framework to incorporate latent variables with non-Euclidean geometry or discrete structure.
Developing more efficient and scalable sparse coding algorithms for large-scale models.
Addressing the binding problem—how multiple objects and attributes are encoded without losing relational information when representations are summed.
papers.abstract: Understanding how information is represented in neural networks is a fundamental challenge in both neuroscience and artificial intelligence. Despite their nonlinear architectures, recent evidence suggests that neural networks encode features in superposition, meaning that input concepts are linearly overlaid within the network's representations. We present a perspective that explains this phenomenon and provides a foundation for extracting interpretable representations from neural activations. Our theoretical framework consists of three steps: (1) Identifiability theory shows that neural networks trained for classification recover latent features up to a linear transformation. (2) Sparse coding methods can extract disentangled features from these representations by leveraging principles from compressed sensing. (3) Quantitative interpretability metrics provide a means to assess the success of these methods, ensuring that extracted features align with human-interpretable concepts. By bridging insights from theoretical neuroscience, representation learning, and interpretability research, we propose an emerging perspective on understanding neural representations in both artificial and biological systems. Our arguments have implications for neural coding theories, AI transparency, and the broader goal of making deep learning models more interpretable.

papers.title: Multifaceted Feature Visualization: Uncovering the Different Types of Features Learned By Each Neuron in Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we visualize the multiple different types of features (facets) that each neuron in a deep neural network responds to, given that neurons are multifaceted?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a Multifaceted Feature Visualization algorithm that uncovers the multiple facets of each neuron and improves activation maximization image quality with more natural colors and coherent global structure.
papers.conclusion: The Multifaceted Feature Visualization algorithm improves the state of the art of activation maximization and provides a more comprehensive understanding of each neuron's function by revealing its multiple facets.
papers.key_findings:
Neurons in deep neural networks are multifaceted, responding to multiple types of features.
Higher-level neurons are more multifaceted than lower-level neurons.
The MFV algorithm produces visualizations with more natural colors and coherent global structure by separately synthesizing each facet.
The algorithm reveals that DNNs learn global structure, details, and context of objects, acting more like generative models.
A center-biased regularization technique reduces the repetition of object fragments in activation maximization images.
papers.limitation:
The number of unique images MFV produces for a unit depends on the manually set k in k-means; automatically identifying the true number of facets remains an open question.
It is unclear whether hidden fully connected layer neurons are truly amalgams of different concepts or part of distributed representations; current visualization methods (Deconv, LRP) do not conclusively reveal this.
future_direction: Future research is needed to understand the precise dynamics of why initializing with a mean facet image improves activation maximization quality.
Automatically identifying the true number of facets per neuron is an important open scientific question.
Further investigation into the function of hidden fully connected layer neurons and whether they are amalgams or represent abstract concepts.
papers.abstract: We can better understand deep neural networks by identifying which features each of their neurons have learned to detect. To do so, researchers have created Deep Visualization techniques including activation maximization, which synthetically generates inputs (e.g. images) that maximally activate each neuron. A limitation of current techniques is that they assume each neuron detects only one type of feature, but we know that neurons can be multifaceted, in that they fire in response to many different types of features: for example, a grocery store class neuron must activate either for rows of produce or for a storefront. Previous activation maximization techniques constructed images without regard for the multiple different facets of a neuron, creating inappropriate mixes of colors, parts of objects, scales, orientations, etc. Here, we introduce an algorithm that explicitly uncovers the multiple facets of each neuron by producing a synthetic visualization of each of the types of images that activate a neuron. We also introduce regularization methods that produce state-of-the-art results in terms of the interpretability of images obtained by activation maximization. By separately synthesizing each type of image a neuron fires in response to, the visualizations have more appropriate colors and coherent global structure. Multifaceted feature visualization thus provides a clearer and more comprehensive description of the role of each neuron.

papers.title: On Identifiability in Transformers
papers.research_question: What is the identifiability of attention weights and token embeddings in Transformers, and how does context aggregate into hidden tokens?
papers.core_contribution: Attention weights are not identifiable and thus not directly interpretable; effective attention and hidden token attribution are proposed as tools to better understand transformers.
papers.conclusion: Attention distributions are not directly interpretable due to non-identifiability; effective attention and hidden token attribution are useful tools for understanding transformers, and the relationship between token mixing and identifiability warrants further investigation.
papers.key_findings:
Attention weights are not identifiable for sequences longer than the attention head dimension, meaning there are infinitely many attention weights yielding the same output.
Effective attention, which removes the null space component, can diverge from raw attention and provide more reliable explanations.
Contextual word embeddings retain their identity (input token) to a large degree across layers, with identity information encoded in the angle.
Input tokens mix strongly in hidden embeddings, with the contribution of the original token decreasing monotonically with depth but remaining the largest individual contributor in most cases.
Context aggregated into hidden embeddings is mostly local, with long-range dependencies increasing in later layers.
papers.limitation:
Effective attention is not guaranteed to be a probability distribution and may have negative weights.
The relationship between token mixing and identifiability warrants further investigation.
future_direction: Further research to understand effective attention and its variants.
Applying the concepts to compare different transformer variants.
papers.abstract: In this paper we delve deep in the Transformer architecture by investigating two of its core components: self-attention and contextual embeddings. In particular, we study the identifiability of attention weights and token embeddings, and the aggregation of context into hidden tokens. We show that, for sequences longer than the attention head dimension, attention weights are not identifiable. We propose effective attention as a complementary tool for improving explanatory interpretations based on attention. Furthermore, we show that input tokens retain to a large degree their identity across the model. We also find evidence suggesting that identity information is mainly encoded in the angle of the embeddings and gradually decreases with depth. Finally, we demonstrate strong mixing of input information in the generation of contextual embeddings by means of a novel quantification method based on gradient attribution. Overall, we show that self-attention distributions are not directly interpretable and present tools to better understand and further investigate Transformer models.

papers.title: Joint learning of interpretation and distillation
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether a distilled model should give a similar prediction for a similar reason as its teacher model on the same input, and proposes methods to explain the distilled model and use explanation imitation to improve distillation.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a novel explanation solution for the GBDT2NN distilled model by using interpretation vectors from the teacher model, and introduces a joint learning method that uses explanation as an auxiliary task to improve prediction performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that imitating the explanation of the teacher model is an effective means to improve the performance of distillation models and provides interpretability for the distilled model.
papers.key_findings:
The independent interpretable method can generate explanations for GBDT2NN that are highly correlated with the teacher model's explanations, as measured by NDCG and top-k coverage.
The joint method, which incorporates interpretation learning into the distillation process, improves the prediction performance of GBDT2NN on several benchmarks.
The joint method also leads to faster convergence during training compared to the standard GBDT2NN model.
Visual evaluation on MNIST datasets shows the proposed method can accurately identify important features (pixels) for classification.
papers.abstract: The extra trust brought by the model interpretation has made it an indispensable part of machine learning systems. But to explain a distilled model's prediction, one may either work with the student model itself, or turn to its teacher model. This leads to a more fundamental question: if a distilled model should give a similar prediction for a similar reason as its teacher model on the same input? This question becomes even more crucial when the two models have dramatically different structure, taking GBDT2NN for example. This paper conducts an empirical study on the new approach to explaining each prediction of GBDT2NN, and how imitating the explanation can further improve the distillation process as an auxiliary learning task. Experiments on several benchmarks show that the proposed methods achieve better performance on both explanations and predictions.

papers.title: Wider Networks Learn Better Features
papers.research_question: How does network width affect the features learned by neural networks, and do wider networks learn more transferable features for novel tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Wider networks learn more informative and transferable features in their hidden states, as visualized by activation atlases, leading to better performance when fine-tuning on novel tasks, even when test accuracy on the original task is independent of width.
papers.conclusion: Wider networks learn more informative features that are beneficial for transfer learning, even when original task performance is unchanged.
papers.key_findings:
Individual neurons in wide networks do not learn interpretable features, but groups of neurons (via activation atlases) do.
Hidden states of wide networks contain more information about inputs than narrow networks, even when test accuracy on the original task is the same.
Fine-tuning a linear classifier on features from a wide network on a new task yields better performance than on narrow networks, even with the same original task accuracy.
The additional information in wide networks (e.g., translation information in translated MNIST) is preserved and useful for transfer.
The features learned by wide networks are distributed across neurons, not sparse.
papers.limitation:
Hyperparameters for wider networks (e.g., learning rate) might be tuned to improve performance on the original task, but this was not explored.
The experiments are conducted on relatively small datasets (MNIST, CIFAR) and network widths, not in the infinite width or lazy training regime.
future_direction: Explore the effect of network width on the performance of transfer learning algorithms like MAML.
Investigate feature learning in the infinite width limit and lazy training regime.
papers.abstract: Transferability of learned features between tasks can massively reduce the cost of training a neural network on a novel task. We investigate the effect of network width on learned features using activation atlases --- a visualization technique that captures features the entire hidden state responds to, as opposed to individual neurons alone. We find that, while individual neurons do not learn interpretable features in wide networks, groups of neurons do. In addition, the hidden state of a wide network contains more information about the inputs than that of a narrow network trained to the same test accuracy. Inspired by this observation, we show that when fine-tuning the last layer of a network on a new task, performance improves significantly as the width of the network is increased, even though test accuracy on the original task is independent of width.

papers.title: Beyond Forgetting: Machine Unlearning Elicits Controllable Side Behaviors and Capabilities
papers.research_question: What are the roles of target vectors in representation misdirection for machine unlearning, and does machine unlearning elicit controllable side behaviors and capabilities beyond forgetting?
papers.core_contribution: Machine unlearning via representation misdirection with concept vectors elicits controllable side behaviors and capabilities, beyond forgetting, which can be a risk or a tool for model control.
papers.conclusion: Machine unlearning can elicit side behaviors and capabilities, which can be either a hidden risk if misused or a mechanism that can be harnessed for developing models with stronger capabilities and controllable behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Unlearning via RAd with truthfulness direction improves model truthfulness on TruthfulQA.
Unlearning via RAd with sentiment direction controls model sentiment on SST2.
Unlearning via RAd with refusal direction induces refusal to harmless instructions in Alpaca.
Unlearning via RAd with task-specific directions improves in-context learning on linguistic and knowledge tasks.
Conversely, RAb with concept directions effectively eliminates these side behaviors.
papers.limitation: RAd models are highly susceptible to benign perturbations, indicating a trade-off between unlearning effectiveness and robustness.
papers.abstract: We consider representation misdirection (RM), a class of LLM unlearning methods that achieves forgetting by manipulating the forget-representations, that is, latent representations of forget samples. Despite being important, the roles of target vectors used in RM, however, remain underexplored. Here, we approach and revisit RM through the lens of the linear representation hypothesis. Specifically, if one can somehow identify a one-dimensional representation corresponding to a high-level concept, the linear representation hypothesis enables linear operations on this concept vector within the forget-representation space. Under this view, we hypothesize that, beyond forgetting, machine unlearning elicits controllable side behaviors and stronger side capabilities corresponding to the high-level concept. Our hypothesis is empirically validated across a wide range of tasks, including behavioral control (e.g., controlling unlearned models' truth, sentiment, and refusal) and capability enhancement (e.g., improving unlearned models' in-context learning capability). Our findings reveal that this fairly attractive phenomenon could be either a hidden risk if misused or a mechanism that can be harnessed for developing models that require stronger capabilities and controllable behaviors.

papers.title: exBERT: A Visual Analysis Tool to Explore Learned Representations in Transformer Models
papers.research_question: How can we develop an interactive tool to explore learned representations and attentions in Transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces EXBERT, an interactive visualization tool for exploring learned representations and attentions in Transformer models, enabling hypothesis formulation and replication of prior analyses.
papers.conclusion: EXBERT is a tool that provides interactive insights into Transformer models' representations and attentions, facilitating hypothesis generation and analysis.
papers.key_findings:
EXBERT can replicate prior findings on BERT's attention heads learning linguistic dependencies such as AUX and POBJ.
BERT's embeddings encode linguistic information progressively across layers, with verbs becoming more prominent in later layers.
EXBERT detects gender bias in GPT-2 by showing that it predicts gendered pronouns based on stereotypical associations.
GPT-2's attention heads learn syntactic structures like AUX and DOBJ dependencies, similar to BERT.
The tool allows for interactive exploration and quick hypothesis testing of model behavior through attention visualization and corpus similarity search.
papers.limitation: EXBERT only presents statistics across a small number of neighbors for a single token at a time, which may not reveal global model behavior.
papers.abstract: Large Transformer-based language models can route and reshape complex information via their multi-headed attention mechanism. Although the attention never receives explicit supervision, it can exhibit recognizable patterns following linguistic or positional information. Analyzing the learned representations and attentions is paramount to furthering our understanding of the inner workings of these models. However, analyses have to catch up with the rapid release of new models and the growing diversity of investigation techniques. To support analysis for a wide variety of models, we introduce EXBERT, a tool to help humans conduct flexible, interactive investigations and formulate hypotheses for the model-internal reasoning process. EXBERT provides insights into the meaning of the contextual representations and attention by matching a humanspecified input to similar contexts in large annotated datasets. By aggregating the annotations of the matched contexts, EXBERT can quickly replicate findings from literature and extend them to previously not analyzed models.

papers.title: Modeling the Influence of Data Structure on Learning in Neural Networks: The Hidden Manifold Model
papers.research_question: How does the structure of data (specifically, data lying on a lower-dimensional manifold) affect the learning dynamics and generalization performance of two-layer neural networks trained with stochastic gradient descent?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Hidden Manifold Model (HMM), a generative model for structured data, and proves a Gaussian Equivalence Property (GEP) that enables analytical derivation of learning dynamics for two-layer neural networks trained with online stochastic gradient descent.
papers.conclusion: The Hidden Manifold Model provides a tractable framework for studying how data structure influences learning in neural networks, and the analytical results offer insights into the dynamics of specialization and generalization.
papers.key_findings:
The Gaussian Equivalence Property holds for the HMM, allowing the learning dynamics to be described by a set of integro-differential equations.
Neural networks learn functions of increasing complexity during training, with a specialization transition where hidden units gradually align with teacher nodes.
Generalization performance deteriorates as the manifold dimension increases and improves with network width, but saturates beyond a certain width.
The learning rate has a minor influence on asymptotic error, but affects the time to reach specialization.
The HMM captures key properties of real data sets (MNIST, CIFAR10) in terms of learning dynamics and memorization patterns.
papers.abstract: Understanding the reasons for the success of deep neural networks trained using stochastic gradientbased methods is a key open problem for the nascent theory of deep learning. The types of data where these networks are most successful, such as images or sequences of speech, are characterized by intricate correlations. Yet, most theoretical work on neural networks does not explicitly model training data or assumes that elements of each data sample are drawn independently from some factorized probability distribution. These approaches are, thus, by construction blind to the correlation structure of real-world datasets and their impact on learning in neural networks. Here, we introduce a generative model for structured datasets that we call the hidden manifold model. The idea is to construct high-dimensional inputs that lie on a lower-dimensional manifold, with labels that depend only on their position within this manifold, akin to a single-layer decoder or generator in a generative adversarial network. We demonstrate that learning of the hidden manifold model is amenable to an analytical treatment by proving a "Gaussian equivalence property" (GEP), and we use the GEP to show how the dynamics of two-layer neural networks trained using one-pass stochastic gradient descent is captured by a set of integro-differential equations that track the performance of the network at all times. This approach permits us to analyze in detail how a neural network learns functions of increasing complexity during training, how its performance depends on its size, and how it is impacted by parameters such as the learning rate or the dimension of the hidden manifold.

papers.title: Towards Understanding Grokking: An Effective Theory of Representation Learning
papers.research_question: What is the origin of generalization in grokking? Why does the training time needed to generalize diverge as training set size decreases? Under what conditions does delayed generalization occur?
papers.core_contribution: Provides an effective theory and phase diagrams to explain grokking, showing that generalization arises from structured representations and that grokking can be understood as a phase between comprehension and memorization.
papers.conclusion: This study provides intuitive explanations of the origin of grokking and highlights the usefulness of physics-inspired tools, such as effective theories and phase diagrams, for understanding deep learning.
papers.key_findings:
Generalization in grokking originates from structured representations, whose dynamics are predicted by an effective theory.
There are four learning phases: comprehension, grokking, memorization, and confusion, with representation learning occurring only in a 'Goldilocks zone'.
On transformers, the grokking phase stays closer to memorization, leading to delayed generalization.
The critical training set size corresponds to the least amount of data needed to determine a good representation.
Grokking can be remedied with proper hyperparameter tuning, as shown in phase diagrams.
papers.limitation: The effective theory is based on Euclidean distance between embeddings and might not capture other metrics defined by the decoder.
