papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether cross-entropy-based supervised learning can invert the data generating process and recover ground-truth latent variables up to a linear transformation under a cluster-centric data generating process.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proves that under a cluster-centric data generating process, cross-entropy-based supervised learning can recover ground-truth latent variables up to a linear transformation, providing a theoretical explanation for the linear representations observed in deep learning models.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that cross-entropy minimization in supervised learning can invert the data generating process and recover latent variables up to linear transformations, offering a unifying theory for the effectiveness of supervised deep learning.
papers.key_findings:
Under the proposed cluster-centric DGP, DIET (parametric instance discrimination) identifies both latent variables and cluster vectors up to linear transformations.
Supervised classification with cross-entropy loss also recovers latent variables up to a linear transformation under the same DGP.
Empirical results on synthetic data confirm the theoretical identifiability when assumptions are met.
On the DisLib benchmark, simple classification tasks recover latent structures up to linear transformations.
On ImageNet-X, pretrained models encode representations that allow linear decoding of proxy factors of variation.
papers.limitation: The theory relies on specific assumptions about the DGP, such as the vMF distribution and cluster structure, which may not hold in real-world data.
future_direction: Extending the theory to more general distributions beyond vMF
Investigating identifiability in the presence of label noise
Applying the insights to improve self-supervised learning algorithms
papers.abstract: Supervised learning has become a cornerstone of modern machine learning, yet a comprehensive theory explaining its effectiveness remains elusive. Empirical phenomena, such as neural analogy-making and the linear representation hypothesis, suggest that supervised models can learn interpretable factors of variation in a linear fashion. Recent advances in self-supervised learning, particularly nonlinear Independent Component Analysis, have shown that these methods can recover latent structures by inverting the data generating process. We extend these identifiability results to parametric instance discrimination, then show how insights transfer to the ubiquitous setting of supervised learning with cross-entropy minimization. We prove that even in standard classification tasks, models learn representations of ground-truth factors of variation up to a linear transformation. We corroborate our theoretical contribution with a series of empirical studies. First, using simulated data matching our theoretical assumptions, we demonstrate successful disentanglement of latent factors. Second, we show that on DisLib, a widely-used disentanglement benchmark, simple classification tasks recover latent structures up to linear transformations. Finally, we reveal that models trained on ImageNet encode representations that permit linear decoding of proxy factors of variation. Together, our theoretical findings and experiments offer a compelling explanation for recent observations of linear representations, such as superposition in neural networks. This work takes a significant step toward a cohesive theory that accounts for the unreasonable effectiveness of supervised deep learning.

papers.title: Eliciting Latent Predictions from Transformers with the Tuned Lens
papers.research_question: How are model predictions refined layer by layer in transformers through iterative inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the tuned lens, a method that trains affine probes to decode hidden states in frozen pretrained transformers, providing more reliable and unbiased prediction trajectories than the logit lens.
papers.conclusion: The tuned lens is a drop-in replacement for the logit lens that provides interpretable prediction trajectories and has applications in anomaly detection and difficulty estimation.
papers.key_findings:
The tuned lens produces lower perplexity and less biased predictions than the logit lens across various models.
Causal experiments show that features influential on the tuned lens are also causally relevant to the model's output.
The tuned lens can detect prompt injection attacks with near-perfect accuracy in some cases.
Prediction depth from the tuned lens correlates with the iteration learned during training, indicating it measures example difficulty.
Tuned lens translators transfer well to fine-tuned models without additional training.
papers.limitation:
Training translators for each layer requires additional computation compared to the logit lens.
Causal basis extraction is computationally intensive.
future_direction: Make causal basis extraction more scalable.
Apply the tuned lens to other modalities beyond language.
papers.abstract: We analyze transformers from the perspective of iterative inference, seeking to understand how model predictions are refined layer by layer. To do so, we train an affine probe for each block in a frozen pretrained model, making it possible to decode every hidden state into a distribution over the vocabulary. Our method, the tuned lens, is a refinement of the earlier "logit lens" technique, which yielded useful insights but is often brittle. We test our method on various autoregressive language models with up to 20B parameters, showing it to be more predictive, reliable and unbiased than the logit lens. With causal experiments, we show the tuned lens uses similar features to the model itself. We also find the trajectory of latent predictions can be used to detect malicious inputs with high accuracy. All code needed to reproduce our results can be found at https://github.com/AlignmentResearch/tuned-lens.

papers.title: Probing Pretrained Language Models for Lexical Semantics
papers.research_question: How can lexical semantic knowledge be extracted from pretrained language models, how is this knowledge distributed across layers, and how do the extracted representations compare to traditional static word embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a systematic study of how to extract type-level lexical semantic knowledge from pretrained language models, showing that monolingual models store rich lexical information primarily in lower layers and that extracted vectors can outperform traditional word embeddings on several monolingual tasks.
papers.conclusion: Pretrained language models store a wealth of type-level lexical knowledge, and effectively uncovering this knowledge depends on careful configuration of extraction strategies, with universal best practices including using monolingual LMs, encoding words with multiple contexts, excluding special tokens, and averaging over lower layers.
papers.key_findings:
Lexical semantic knowledge is concentrated in the lower Transformer layers of pretrained language models.
Averaging representations across multiple layers yields better performance than using a single layer.
Monolingual language models contain more lexical information for a target language than massively multilingual models like mBERT.
Extracted 'BERT-based' static word embeddings outperform fastText on monolingual tasks (e.g., lexical similarity, analogy, relation prediction) but not on cross-lingual tasks (BLI, CLIR).
Translation pairs obtain similar representations in independently trained monolingual LMs, indicating approximate isomorphism between the monolingual spaces.
papers.limitation: The comparison with fastText word embeddings is not strictly apples-to-apples because the models were trained on different corpora (Wikipedia dumps for fastText vs. the corpora used for pretraining the LMs).
future_direction: Investigating how domains of external corpora affect the extraction of word representations and how to sample representative contexts.
Extending the study to more languages, more lexical semantic probes, and other larger underlying language models.
Developing more sophisticated lexical representation extraction methods, such as layer weighting or attention, and lightweight methods to enrich lexical content in multilingual LMs.
papers.abstract: The success of large pretrained language models (LMs) such as BERT and RoBERTa has sparked interest in probing their representations, in order to unveil what types of knowledge they implicitly capture. While prior research focused on morphosyntactic, semantic, and world knowledge, it remains unclear to which extent LMs also derive lexical type-level knowledge from words in context. In this work, we present a systematic empirical analysis across six typologically diverse languages and five different lexical tasks, addressing the following questions: 1) How do different lexical knowledge extraction strategies (monolingual versus multilingual source LM, out-ofcontext versus in-context encoding, inclusion of special tokens, and layer-wise averaging) impact performance? How consistent are the observed effects across tasks and languages? 2) Is lexical knowledge stored in few parameters, or is it scattered throughout the network? 3) How do these representations fare against traditional static word vectors in lexical tasks? 4) Does the lexical information emerging from independently trained monolingual LMs display latent similarities? Our main results indicate patterns and best practices that hold universally, but also point to prominent variations across languages and tasks. Moreover, we validate the claim that lower Transformer layers carry more type-level lexical knowledge, but also show that this knowledge is distributed across multiple layers.

papers.title: Learning Important Features Through Propagating Activation Differences
papers.research_question: How can we assign importance scores to the inputs of a neural network for a given output by comparing activations to a reference and propagating differences?
papers.core_contribution: Presents DeepLIFT, a method for decomposing neural network predictions by backpropagating contributions of neurons to input features using a difference-from-reference approach, which can handle saturation and discontinuities, and optionally separates positive and negative contributions to reveal dependencies.
papers.conclusion: DeepLIFT is a novel approach for computing importance scores based on explaining differences from a reference, which can propagate information when gradients are zero and avoid misleading importance on bias terms, and the RevealCancel rule can identify dependencies missed by other methods.
papers.key_findings:
DeepLIFT can propagate importance signals even when the gradient is zero, addressing saturation problems.
DeepLIFT avoids artifacts caused by discontinuous gradients, such as misleading importance on bias terms.
The RevealCancel rule, which separately treats positive and negative contributions, can identify dependencies missed by other methods, as demonstrated in the min(i1,i2) example.
On MNIST, DeepLIFT with RevealCancel outperforms gradient-based methods in a pixel erasure task designed to convert digits from one class to another.
On simulated genomic data, DeepLIFT with RevealCancel on the fully-connected layer and Rescale on convolutional layers reduces noise and correctly identifies motif cooperativity, while other methods fail in certain aspects.
papers.limitation:
How to apply DeepLIFT to RNNs is an open question.
How to compute a good reference empirically from the data is an open question.
How to propagate importance through 'max' operations (as in Maxout or Maxpooling neurons) beyond simply using gradients is an open question.
future_direction: Applying DeepLIFT to RNNs
Computing a good reference empirically from the data
Propagating importance through 'max' operations
papers.abstract: The purported "black box" nature of neural networks is a barrier to adoption in applications where interpretability is essential. Here we present DeepLIFT (Deep Learning Important FeaTures), a method for decomposing the output prediction of a neural network on a specific input by backpropagating the contributions of all neurons in the network to every feature of the input. DeepLIFT compares the activation of each neuron to its 'reference activation' and assigns contribution scores according to the difference. By optionally giving separate consideration to positive and negative contributions, DeepLIFT can also reveal dependencies which are missed by other approaches. Scores can be computed efficiently in a single backward pass. We apply DeepLIFT to models trained on MNIST and simulated genomic data, and show significant advantages over gradient-based methods. Video tutorial: http://goo.gl/qKb7pL, ICML slides: bit.ly/deeplifticmlslides, ICML talk: https://vimeo.com/238275076, code: http://goo.gl/RM8jvH.

papers.title: Image denoising with multi-layer perceptrons, part 2: training trade-offs and analysis of their mechanisms
papers.research_question: What trade-offs must be considered when training multi-layer perceptrons for image denoising, and how do these networks internally achieve denoising?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides detailed guidelines for training MLPs to achieve state-of-the-art image denoising and analyzes their inner workings, showing that denoising is achieved through saturation of the tanh activation function, leading to binary hidden representations.
papers.conclusion: MLPs can achieve excellent image denoising performance when trained with appropriate trade-offs, and their internal mechanisms can be understood through analysis of hidden unit activation patterns, revealing a denoising process based on saturation and binary codes.
papers.key_findings:
More training data and more hidden units per layer consistently improve performance.
There exists an ideal number of hidden layers; too many layers, especially in deep and narrow networks, can cause catastrophic performance degradation.
Fine-tuning with a lower learning rate after initial training reduces test error fluctuations and improves final performance.
Denoising in single-hidden-layer MLPs is achieved through saturation of the tanh layer, which attenuates noise while preserving features detected by highly active neurons.
The feature detectors (input weights) adapt to the noise type and strength; for example, larger input patches are learned for stronger noise.
papers.limitation:
Deep and narrow networks (with many hidden layers but few units per layer) are difficult to optimize and can suffer catastrophic degradation in performance.
Block-matching MLPs do not provide a clear advantage at very low or very high noise levels, and their performance can deteriorate compared to plain MLPs at high noise levels.
future_direction: Applying similar training guidelines and analysis to other image processing tasks like super-resolution, deconvolution, and demosaicking.
Exploring the benefits of binary representations compared to sparse representations in deep networks.
papers.abstract: Image denoising can be described as the problem of mapping from a noisy image to a noise-free image. In another paper, we show that multi-layer perceptrons can achieve outstanding image denoising performance for various types of noise (additive white Gaussian noise, mixed Poisson-Gaussian noise, JPEG artifacts, salt-and-pepper noise and noise resembling stripes). In this work we discuss in detail which trade-offs have to be considered during the training procedure. We will show how to achieve good results and which pitfalls to avoid. By analysing the activation patterns of the hidden units we are able to make observations regarding the functioning principle of multi-layer perceptrons trained for image denoising.

papers.title: Emergent World Representations: Exploring a Sequence Model Trained on a Synthetic Task
papers.research_question: Does a sequence model trained on a synthetic task (Othello game transcripts) learn an internal representation of the board state, and is that representation causal to its predictions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that a GPT model trained on Othello game transcripts learns a nonlinear internal representation of the board state, which is causally involved in its predictions. It introduces intervention techniques and latent saliency maps for interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The experiments provide evidence that Othello-GPT maintains a nonlinear internal representation of the game board state, which is causally linked to its predictions. The tools introduced (nonlinear probes, interventions, latent saliency maps) may prove useful for interpretability in natural language settings.
papers.key_findings:
Othello-GPT predicts legal moves with high accuracy, and this is not due to memorization.
Nonlinear probes can accurately decode the board state from internal activations, while linear probes perform poorly.
Intervention experiments show that the board representation is causal to the model's predictions.
Latent saliency maps reveal differences between models trained on synthetic vs. championship data, indicating different learned strategies.
The internal representation of the board state is nonlinear and emerges during training.
papers.limitation: Latent saliency maps only attribute to one tile when multiple tiles are involved in a move, which does not fully capture the Othello rule logic.
future_direction: Extend investigation to other, more complex games.
Compare strategies learned by a sequence model with those of a model trained with a priori knowledge of Othello.
Study how results generalize to natural language models.
papers.abstract: Language models show a surprising range of capabilities, but the source of their apparent competence is unclear. Do these networks just memorize a collection of surface statistics, or do they rely on internal representations of the process that generates the sequences they see? We investigate this question by applying a variant of the GPT model to the task of predicting legal moves in a simple board game, Othello. Although the network has no a priori knowledge of the game or its rules, we uncover evidence of an emergent nonlinear internal representation of the board state. Interventional experiments indicate this representation can be used to control the output of the network and create "latent saliency maps" that can help explain predictions in human terms.

papers.title: A Closer Look at Deep Learning Heuristics: Learning rate restarts, Warmup and Distillation
papers.research_question: Why do heuristics such as cosine annealing (SGDR), learning rate warmup, and knowledge distillation improve the convergence and performance of deep learning models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uses mode connectivity and canonical correlation analysis (CCA) to empirically investigate the reasons behind the success of deep learning heuristics like cosine annealing, learning rate warmup, and knowledge distillation.
papers.conclusion: The empirical analysis using mode connectivity and CCA sheds light on the heuristics of cosine annealing, warmup, and distillation, suggesting that common explanations are oversimplified and opening new questions for deeper exploration.
papers.key_findings:
The reasons often quoted for the success of cosine annealing (e.g., escaping local minima) are not evidenced in practice; iterates move over barriers after restarts but this is an oversimplification.
The effect of learning rate warmup is to prevent the deeper layers (e.g., fully-connected stack) from creating training instability; freezing these layers achieves similar outcomes.
In knowledge distillation, the latent knowledge shared by the teacher is primarily disbursed to the deeper layers of the student network.
Mode connectivity is a robust framework for connecting optima obtained from vastly different training schemes (e.g., different optimizers, batch sizes, regularization).
For SGDR, the path found by mode connectivity corresponds to lower training loss but higher validation loss than the iterates, suggesting a generalization gap.
papers.abstract: The convergence rate and final performance of common deep learning models have significantly benefited from heuristics such as learning rate schedules, knowledge distillation, skip connections, and normalization layers. In the absence of theoretical underpinnings, controlled experiments aimed at explaining these strategies can aid our understanding of deep learning landscapes and the training dynamics. Existing approaches for empirical analysis rely on tools of linear interpolation and visualizations with dimensionality reduction, each with their limitations. Instead, we revisit such analysis of heuristics through the lens of recently proposed methods for loss surface and representation analysis, viz., mode connectivity and canonical correlation analysis (CCA), and hypothesize reasons for the success of the heuristics. In particular, we explore knowledge distillation and learning rate heuristics of (cosine) restarts and warmup using mode connectivity and CCA. Our empirical analysis suggests that: (a) the reasons often quoted for the success of cosine annealing are not evidenced in practice; (b) that the effect of learning rate warmup is to prevent the deeper layers from creating training instability; and (c) that the latent knowledge shared by the teacher is primarily disbursed to the deeper layers.

papers.title: Natural language instructions induce compositional generalization in networks of neurons
papers.research_question: What neural computations allow networks to interpret linguistic instructions and perform novel tasks without explicit experience?
papers.core_contribution: Language instructions enable zero-shot generalization in neural networks by aligning sensorimotor representations with the semantic geometry of instructions, allowing composition of practiced skills for novel tasks.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates how linguistic instructions induce compositional generalization in neural networks, offering testable predictions for neural representations underlying flexible cognition in the human brain.
papers.key_findings:
Models using sentence-level semantics (e.g., SBERT) achieve up to 83% correct zero-shot generalization on unseen tasks.
Language scaffolds sensorimotor representations such that their geometry shares structure with instruction embeddings, facilitating compositionality.
Individual neurons in the sensorimotor network modulate their tuning based on the semantics of instructions.
The network can produce linguistic descriptions of novel tasks based solely on motor feedback, enabling knowledge transfer to partner models.
Generalization is supported by cross-condition generalization performance (CCGP) metrics that correlate with task performance.
future_direction: Guiding imaging studies to delineate brain areas involved in instruction following
Comparing compositional representations in nonlinguistic subjects like nonhuman primates
papers.abstract: A fundamental human cognitive feat is to interpret linguistic instructions in order to perform novel tasks without explicit task experience. Yet, the neural computations that might be used to accomplish this remain poorly understood. We use advances in natural language processing to create a neural model of generalization based on linguistic instructions. Models are trained on a set of common psychophysical tasks, and receive instructions embedded by a pretrained language model. Our best models can perform a previously unseen task with an average performance of 83% correct based solely on linguistic instructions (that is, zero-shot learning). We found that language scaffolds sensorimotor representations such that activity for interrelated tasks shares a common geometry with the semantic representations of instructions, allowing language to cue the proper composition of practiced skills in unseen settings. We show how this model generates a linguistic description of a novel task it has identified using only motor feedback, which can subsequently guide a partner model to perform the task. Our models offer several experimentally testable predictions outlining how linguistic information must be represented to facilitate flexible and general cognition in the human brain.

papers.title: Microscopic and collective signatures of feature learning in neural networks
papers.research_question: What are the collective and microscopic signatures of feature learning in Bayesian shallow neural networks in the proportional regime?
papers.core_contribution: In the proportional regime, feature learning in Bayesian shallow neural networks is characterized by a nonmonotonic distance between class manifolds and finite, data-dependent weight correlations.
papers.conclusion: The squared distance between class manifolds and the finite weight correlations are collective and microscopic signatures of feature learning in Bayesian shallow networks in the proportional regime.
papers.key_findings:
The posterior distance between class manifolds remains unaltered in the infinite-width limit but departs from its prior value at proportional width.
The average squared distance is a nonmonotonic function of temperature, and this nonmonotonicity disappears in the infinite-width limit or when labels are randomized.
The hidden-layer weights become correlated in the proportional regime, undergoing a finite displacement.
The nonmonotonicity of the distance aligns with inversion dynamics observed during gradient descent training, serving as an equilibrium counterpart.
The second-order statistics of the weights depends on input patterns in a way not traceable to the infinite-width limit.
papers.limitation:
The results are limited to standard-scaled neural networks and do not apply to mean-field scaling.
The theory does not characterize feature learning closer to the interpolation threshold.
papers.abstract: Feature extraction - the ability to identify relevant properties of data - is a key factor underlying the success of deep learning. Yet, it has proved difficult to elucidate its nature within existing predictive theories, to the extent that there is no consensus on the very definition of feature learning. A promising hint in this direction comes from previous phenomenological observations of quasi-universal aspects in the training dynamics of neural networks, displayed by simple properties of feature geometry. We address this problem within a statistical-mechanics framework for Bayesian learning in one hidden layer neural networks with standard parameterization. Analytical computations in the proportional limit (when both the network width and the size of the training set are large) can quantify fingerprints of feature learning, both collective ones (related to manifold geometry) and microscopic ones (related to the weights). In particular, (i) the distance between different class manifolds in feature space is a nonmonotonic function of the temperature, which we interpret as the equilibrium counterpart of a phenomenon observed under gradient descent (GD) dynamics, and (ii) the microscopic learnable parameters in the network undergo a finite data-dependent displacement with respect to the infinite-width limit, and develop correlations. These results indicate that nontrivial feature learning is at play in a regime where the posterior predictive distribution is that of Gaussian process regression with a trivially rescaled prior.

papers.title: Its Alive: AI Independence Without Human Prompting
papers.research_question: How can representation engineering (RepE) improve transparency and control of AI systems, particularly for safety-relevant concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces representation engineering (RepE) as a top-down approach to AI transparency, providing baselines like Linear Artificial Tomography (LAT) and demonstrating its applicability to reading and controlling safety-relevant concepts in large language models.
papers.conclusion: RepE is a promising top-down approach for enhancing AI transparency and control, with broad applicability to safety-relevant problems, and can accelerate progress in AI safety.
papers.key_findings:
RepE methods can extract representations of high-level concepts like honesty, utility, emotion, and harmfulness.
LAT achieves state-of-the-art on TruthfulQA, improving zero-shot accuracy by 18.1 percentage points.
Representation control can increase model honesty and reduce compliance with harmful instructions, even under jailbreak attempts.
Emotions are represented in LLMs and can be manipulated to affect model compliance and behavior.
RepE provides traction on inner alignment problems like deceptive alignment by enabling monitoring and control of honesty.
future_direction: Further exploration of RepE for transparency and safety of AI systems.
Investigation of emotion representations and their impact on model behavior and concept of self.
Improving robustness and generalization of RepE methods.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we identify and characterize the emerging area of representation engineering (RepE), an approach to enhancing the transparency of AI systems that draws on insights from cognitive neuroscience. RepE places population-level representations, rather than neurons or circuits, at the center of analysis, equipping us with novel methods for monitoring and manipulating high-level cognitive phenomena in deep neural networks (DNNs). We provide baselines and an initial analysis of RepE techniques, showing that they offer simple yet effective solutions for improving our understanding and control of large language models. We showcase how these methods can provide traction on a wide range of safety-relevant problems, including honesty, harmlessness, power-seeking, and more, demonstrating the promise of top-down transparency research. We hope that this work catalyzes further exploration of RepE and fosters advancements in the transparency and safety of AI systems.

papers.title: Accurate Word Alignment Induction from Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: Do attention weights in Transformer models capture accurate word alignments, and how can word alignments be better induced from neural machine translation models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that Transformer attention weights can capture accurate word alignments if the correct decoding step and layer are chosen, and introduces two novel methods (SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET) that induce alignments at the step when the target token is the decoder input, significantly improving alignment accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The proposed methods SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET effectively induce word alignments from Transformer models, with SHIFT-AET achieving state-of-the-art performance without compromising translation quality.
papers.key_findings:
SHIFT-ATT, a pure interpretation method, reduces AER by 7.0-10.2 points over the NAIVE-ATT baseline and 5.5-7.9 points over FAST-ALIGN on three datasets.
SHIFT-AET, which adds and trains an alignment module supervised by SHIFT-ATT alignments, outperforms the statistical aligner GIZA++ by 1.4-4.8 AER points.
A proposed layer selection criterion, based on agreement between source-to-target and target-to-source model alignments, effectively identifies the best layer for alignment induction.
Both SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET improve performance on the downstream task of dictionary-guided decoding compared to the NAIVE-ATT baseline.
Probing experiments show decoder hidden states at lower layers are more relevant to the input token than the output token, validating the shift in alignment step.
future_direction: Extend the study to more downstream tasks and systems.
papers.abstract: Despite its original goal to jointly learn to align and translate, prior researches suggest that Transformer captures poor word alignments through its attention mechanism. In this paper, we show that attention weights DO capture accurate word alignments and propose two novel word alignment induction methods SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET. The main idea is to induce alignments at the step when the to-be-aligned target token is the decoder input rather than the decoder output as in previous work. SHIFT-ATT is an interpretation method that induces alignments from the attention weights of Transformer and does not require parameter update or architecture change. SHIFT-AET extracts alignments from an additional alignment module which is tightly integrated into Transformer and trained in isolation with supervision from symmetrized SHIFT-ATT alignments. Experiments on three publicly available datasets demonstrate that both methods perform better than their corresponding neural baselines and SHIFT-AET significantly outperforms GIZA++ by 1.4-4.8 AER points.

papers.title: Attribution-Guided Distillation of Matryoshka Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we distill a compact, reusable core of consistently useful features from Matryoshka Sparse Autoencoders to improve feature consistency and transferability across training runs and sparsity levels?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DMSAEs, an attribution-guided training pipeline that distills a compact, reusable core of latent features from Matryoshka SAEs, improving feature consistency and transferability across sparsity levels.
papers.conclusion: DMSAEs provide a practical route toward feature consistency across SAEs and transferability of interpretations across training runs and sparsity levels.
papers.key_findings:
Seven cycles of distillation on Gemma-2-2B layer 12 activations yielded a distilled core of 197 features that were repeatedly selected.
Training SAEs using the distilled core improves several SAEBench metrics, including absorption and RAVEL, compared to Matryoshka SAE baselines.
The method demonstrates that consistent sets of latent features can be transferred across sparsity levels.
Attribution-guided distillation identifies core latents that remain systematically useful for reconstruction, unlike a randomly initialized core which is driven towards zero activity.
papers.limitation:
Requires multiple cycles of distillation, leading to much higher computational costs relative to training a single Matryoshka SAE.
Core selection depends on the gradient × activation attribution method, which is a fast first-order approximation but may be suboptimal.
Freezing encoder weight vectors stabilizes detection directions, but encoder biases and decoder weights are reinitialized, so latent behavior (threshold, firing rate, contribution) can still change across cycles.
future_direction: Reducing the computational cost of distillation.
Extending the DMSAE framework to other models and scientific domains.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) aim to disentangle model activations into monosemantic, human-interpretable features. In practice, learned features are often redundant and vary across training runs and sparsity levels, which makes interpretations difficult to transfer and reuse. We introduce Distilled Matryoshka Sparse Autoencoders (DMSAEs), a training pipeline that distills a compact core of consistently useful features and reuses it to train new SAEs. DMSAEs run an iterative distillation cycle: train a Matryoshka SAE with a shared core, use gradient X activation to measure each feature's contribution to next-token loss in the most nested reconstruction, and keep only the smallest subset that explains a fixed fraction of the attribution. Only the core encoder weight vectors are transferred across cycles; the core decoder and all non-core latents are reinitialized each time. On Gemma-2-2B layer 12 residual stream activations, seven cycles of distillation (500M tokens, 65k width) yielded a distilled core of 197 features that were repeatedly selected. Training using this distilled core improves several SAEBench metrics and demonstrates that consistent sets of latent features can be transferred across sparsity levels

papers.title: A Theoretical Analysis on Feature Learning in Neural Networks: Emergence from Inputs and Advantage over Fixed Features
papers.research_question: How can effective features emerge from inputs in the training dynamics of gradient descent? Is learning features from inputs necessary for the superior performance of neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Theoretical analysis proves that feature learning in neural networks emerges from input structure via gradient descent, providing an advantage over fixed-feature models.
papers.conclusion: Feature learning in neural networks depends strongly on the input structure and leads to superior performance.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks trained by gradient descent can learn effective features from input data structure.
Feature learning involves emergence and improvement of features through gradient steps.
Linear models on data-independent fixed features require exponentially large models to achieve similar performance.
Without the input structure, no polynomial-time algorithm in the Statistical Query model can learn effectively.
Experiments on synthetic and real data support the theoretical findings.
papers.limitation: The problem setup does not include hierarchical representations, which are important in practical data.
future_direction: Extend analysis to hierarchical representations in data.
Further studies on modeling input structure and analyzing feature learning.
papers.abstract: An important characteristic of neural networks is their ability to learn representations of the input data with effective features for prediction, which is believed to be a key factor to their superior empirical performance. To better understand the source and benefit of feature learning in neural networks, we consider learning problems motivated by practical data, where the labels are determined by a set of class relevant patterns and the inputs are generated from these along with some background patterns. We prove that neural networks trained by gradient descent can succeed on these problems. The success relies on the emergence and improvement of effective features, which are learned among exponentially many candidates efficiently by exploiting the data (in particular, the structure of the input distribution). In contrast, no linear models on data-independent features of polynomial sizes can learn to as good errors. Furthermore, if the specific input structure is removed, then no polynomial algorithm in the Statistical Query model can learn even weakly. These results provide theoretical evidence showing that feature learning in neural networks depends strongly on the input structure and leads to the superior performance. Our preliminary experimental results on synthetic and real data also provide positive support.

papers.title: All Bark and No Bite: Rogue Dimensions in Transformer Language Models Obscure Representational Quality
papers.research_question: How informative are standard similarity measures (cosine similarity, Euclidean distance) in contextualized language models, and how do rogue dimensions dominate these measures, obscuring representational quality?
papers.core_contribution: Standard similarity measures in contextual language models are dominated by a small number of rogue dimensions, and simple postprocessing techniques like standardization can correct for this, revealing underlying representational quality that is preserved across all layers.
papers.conclusion: Standard similarity measures are not informative for contextual language models due to rogue dimensions, and accounting for these dimensions (e.g., via standardization) is essential for any similarity-based analysis.
papers.key_findings:
A small number of rogue dimensions (1-5) dominate cosine similarity and Euclidean distance in contextual language models.
Rogue dimensions are centered far from the origin and have disproportionately high variance.
The rogue dimensions that dominate similarity measures do not dominate model behavior; ablating them has little effect on the language modeling distribution.
Rogue dimensions are often correlated with specific tokens (e.g., punctuation) and positions (e.g., position zero).
After postprocessing (e.g., standardization), representational quality (correlation with human similarity judgments) improves and is preserved across all layers, contrary to previous claims of degradation in later layers.
future_direction: Designing and implementing language models that do not develop rogue dimensions in the first place.
Understanding how rogue dimensions arise over time during pretraining.
Using the MultiBERT checkpoints to study whether rogue dimensions are coincidental or requisite for good performance, and how they emerge.
papers.abstract: Similarity measures are a vital tool for understanding how language models represent and process language. Standard representational similarity measures such as cosine similarity and Euclidean distance have been successfully used in static word embedding models to understand how words cluster in semantic space. Recently, these measures have been applied to embeddings from contextualized models such as BERT and GPT-2. In this work, we call into question the informativity of such measures for contextualized language models. We find that a small number of rogue dimensions, often just 1-3, dominate these measures. Moreover, we find a striking mismatch between the dimensions that dominate similarity measures and those which are important to the behavior of the model. We show that simple postprocessing techniques such as standardization are able to correct for rogue dimensions and reveal underlying representational quality. We argue that accounting for rogue dimensions is essential for any similarity-based analysis of contextual language models.

papers.title: From Low-Rank Features to Encoding Mismatch: Rethinking Feature Distillation in Vision Transformers
papers.research_question: Why does feature-map knowledge distillation (KD), which works so well for CNNs, usually fail for Vision Transformers (ViTs)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies an encoding mismatch between wide teachers and narrow students in Vision Transformers as the reason for the failure of feature-map knowledge distillation, and proposes two minimal strategies (post-hoc feature lifting and native width alignment) to resolve this mismatch, reactivating simple feature distillation.
papers.conclusion: The encoding mismatch is the key reason for the failure of feature distillation in ViTs, and the proposed strategies effectively resolve this mismatch, providing a simple and interpretable design cue for compact ViT architectures.
papers.key_findings:
ViT representations are globally low-rank, with a small number of singular components capturing most of the feature energy.
Despite global low-rank structure, individual tokens use a high fraction of channel capacity, leading to an encoding mismatch between wide teachers and narrow students.
This encoding mismatch explains why naive feature-map distillation fails in ViTs.
Two proposed strategies (post-hoc feature lifting and native width alignment) reactivate feature distillation, improving DeiT-Tiny accuracy by up to 3.37% when distilling from CaiT-S24.
The architectural modifications also improve standalone student performance without distillation, indicating a genuine bottleneck in compact ViTs.
papers.abstract: Feature-map knowledge distillation (KD) is highly effective for convolutional networks but often fails for Vision Transformers (ViTs). To understand this failure and guide method design, we conduct a two-view representation analysis of ViTs. First, a layer-wise Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) of full feature matrices shows that final-layer representations are globally low-rank: for CaiT-S24, only $121/61/34/14$ dimensions suffice to capture $99\%/95\%/90\%/80\%$ of the energy. In principle, this suggests that a compact student plus a simple linear projector should be enough for feature alignment, contradicting the weak empirical performance of standard feature KD. To resolve this paradox, we introduce a token-level Spectral Energy Pattern (SEP) analysis that measures how each token uses channel capacity. SEP reveals that, despite the global low-rank structure, individual tokens distribute energy over most channels, forming a high-bandwidth encoding pattern. This results in an encoding mismatch between wide teachers and narrow students. Motivated by this insight, we propose two minimal, mismatch-driven strategies: (1) post-hoc feature lifting with a lightweight projector retained during inference, or (2) native width alignment that widens only the student's last block to the teacher's width. On ImageNet-1K, these strategies reactivate simple feature-map distillation in ViTs, raising DeiT-Tiny accuracy from $74.86\%$ to $77.53\%$ and $78.23\%$ when distilling from CaiT-S24, while also improving standalone students trained without any teacher. Our analysis thus explains why ViT feature distillation fails and shows how exploiting low-rank structure yields effective, interpretable remedies and concrete design guidance for compact ViTs.

papers.title: Emergent Linear Representations in World Models of Self-Supervised Sequence Models
papers.research_question: What is the nature of feature representations in sequence models? Specifically, are world models linearly encoded in the activation space?
papers.core_contribution: The board state in OthelloGPT is linearly encoded relative to the current player (MINE vs. YOURS), enabling control of the model's behavior via simple vector arithmetic.
papers.conclusion: The emergent world model in OthelloGPT is linearly represented, enabling interpretability and control via vector arithmetic, and revealing multiple circuits and iterative refinement across layers.
papers.key_findings:
OthelloGPT linearly encodes the board state relative to the current player (MINE/YOURS) rather than absolute colors, achieving high accuracy with linear probes.
Simple vector addition of linear directions (MINE, YOURS, EMPTY) to the residual stream can causally alter the model's believed board state and move predictions.
The model also linearly encodes which tiles are flipped at each timestep, as shown by high F1 scores with linear probes.
Evidence suggests multiple circuits exist: in end games, legal moves are sometimes computed before the full board state is accurately represented.
The model iteratively refines board state and move predictions across layers, with accuracy improving layer by layer.
papers.limitation:
Probing requires knowing which features to look for, and human preconceptions may lead to incorrect interpretations.
The model's board state accuracy drops in end games, and it may use alternative circuits, indicating incomplete understanding.
future_direction: Investigate why linear feature representations emerge and what linear representations exist in large language models.
papers.abstract: How do sequence models represent their decision-making process? Prior work suggests that Othello-playing neural network learned nonlinear models of the board state (Li et al., 2023a). In this work, we provide evidence of a closely related linear representation of the board. In particular, we show that probing for "my colour" vs. "opponent's colour" may be a simple yet powerful way to interpret the model's internal state. This precise understanding of the internal representations allows us to control the model's behaviour with simple vector arithmetic. Linear representations enable significant interpretability progress, which we demonstrate with further exploration of how the world model is computed.

papers.title: Latent Introspection: Models Can Detect Prior Concept Injections
papers.research_question: Can language models access information about their own prior internal states? Specifically, can they detect when concepts have been injected into their earlier context and identify which concept was injected?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that open-weight language models possess a latent capacity for introspection, enabling them to detect prior concept injections. This ability is often hidden in the residual stream and can be dramatically strengthened through specific prompting.
papers.conclusion: Language models have a surprising capacity for introspection and steering awareness that is easy to overlook, with consequences for latent reasoning and safety.
papers.key_findings:
Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct can detect prior concept injections, with detection signals emerging in middle layers (50–60) but attenuating in the final layers before output.
Prompting the model with accurate information about AI introspection mechanisms can increase detection sensitivity from 0.3% to 39.9% with only a 0.6% increase in false positives.
The model can identify which of nine concepts was injected earlier, with mutual information between injected and recovered concepts rising from 0.61 bits to 1.05 bits, ruling out generic noise explanations.
Detection capacity varies dramatically with prompting; a vague framing outperforms a mechanistically accurate description, achieving up to 84.0% accuracy.
The phenomenon generalizes to larger models (Llama 3.3 70B Instruct and Qwen 2.5 72B Instruct), though with different prompt sensitivities and signal strengths.
papers.limitation: The introspection signals are suppressed in the final layers of the model, which may be due to post-training effects (e.g., safety training), pretraining factors, or distribution shift.
future_direction: Distinguishing the causes of late-layer suppression (post-training vs. pretraining effects).
Mechanistic investigation of why vague framing outperforms accurate description in prompting.
papers.abstract: We uncover a latent capacity for introspection in a Qwen 32B model, demonstrating that the model can detect when concepts have been injected into its earlier context and identify which concept was injected. While the model denies injection in sampled outputs, logit lens analysis reveals clear detection signals in the residual stream, which are attenuated in the final layers. Furthermore, prompting the model with accurate information about AI introspection mechanisms can dramatically strengthen this effect: the sensitivity to injection increases massively (0.3% -> 39.2%) with only a 0.6% increase in false positives. Also, mutual information between nine injected and recovered concepts rises from 0.62 bits to 1.05 bits, ruling out generic noise explanations. Our results demonstrate models can have a surprising capacity for introspection and steering awareness that is easy to overlook, with consequences for latent reasoning and safety.

papers.title: Language Through a Prism: A Spectral Approach for Multiscale Language\n Representations
papers.research_question: To what extent do deep models capture information at different scales (from subwords to documents), and can we force them to better capture structure across this hierarchy?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a spectral filtering framework to disentangle scale-specific information in language model representations and a prism layer that trains models to specialize neurons for different scales, improving performance on long-range tasks.
papers.conclusion: Spectral techniques are a powerful set of tools for uncovering and modeling multiscale phenomena in deep NLP models.
papers.key_findings:
Spectral filters can disentangle scale-specific information in BERT representations, with high-pass filters useful for word-level tasks and low-pass filters for document-level tasks.
The prism layer enables BERT to produce multiscale representations that improve performance on utterance- and document-level tasks while maintaining word-level performance.
Training with the prism layer increases the model's sensitivity to long-range context in masked language modeling.
The method is general and could be applied to other domains like images, audio, and video.
future_direction: Applying the spectral techniques to other domains such as computer vision, time series, and reinforcement learning models.
Using the tools for interpretability research to better understand knowledge and information processing at different scales.
Applying the method to track topics over time in linguistic change research.
papers.abstract:
Language exhibits structure at different scales, ranging from subwords to
words, sentences, paragraphs, and documents. To what extent do deep models
capture information at these scales, and can we force them to better capture
structure across this hierarchy? We approach this question by focusing on
individual neurons, analyzing the behavior of their activations at different
timescales. We show that signal processing provides a natural framework for
separating structure across scales, enabling us to 1) disentangle
scale-specific information in existing embeddings and 2) train models to learn
more about particular scales. Concretely, we apply spectral filters to the
activations of a neuron across an input, producing filtered embeddings that
perform well on part of speech tagging (word-level), dialog speech acts
classification (utterance-level), or topic classification (document-level),
while performing poorly on the other tasks. We also present a prism layer for
training models, which uses spectral filters to constrain different neurons to
model structure at different scales. Our proposed BERT + Prism model can better
predict masked tokens using long-range context and produces multiscale
representations that perform better at utterance- and document-level tasks. Our
methods are general and readily applicable to other domains besides language,
such as images, audio, and video.

papers.title: Collective variables of neural networks: empirical time evolution and scaling laws
papers.research_question: How can the entropy and trace of the empirical neural tangent kernel (NTK) be used to understand learning dynamics and scaling relations in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces entropy and trace of the empirical neural tangent kernel as collective variables to analyze neural network training dynamics, identifying two learning regimes (information compression and structure formation) and showing that structure formation characterizes the deep learning regime.
papers.conclusion: Entropy and trace of the NTK provide a universal framework for understanding neural network learning dynamics and scaling, with structure formation identified as a hallmark of deep learning.
papers.key_findings:
Entropy of the NTK reveals two learning regimes: information compression (entropy decreases) where gradient vectors align, and structure formation (entropy increases) where the network separates data to create richer representations.
Small networks tend to remain in the compression regime with limited performance, while large networks transition to structure formation, which is associated with improved performance and defines a deep learning regime.
The trace of the NTK, representing an effective learning rate, increases during training, indicating growing network sensitivity to new data and potential vulnerabilities to adversarial attacks or benefits for continual learning.
The dynamics observed via entropy and trace are universal across diverse architectures including transformers, GNNs, CNNs, and reinforcement learning agents.
Architecture scaling (width and depth) influences the entropy and trace, with deeper networks showing reduced entropy at initialization but capable of achieving higher entropy after training when sufficiently wide.
future_direction: Explore how scaling behavior for different activation functions can be used for targeted architecture selection.
Investigate the trace property to reduce model sensitivity and improve continual learning strategies.
Explore avenues for improved stability by reducing trace late in training.
papers.abstract: This work presents a novel means for understanding learning dynamics and scaling relations in neural networks. We show that certain measures on the spectrum of the empirical neural tangent kernel, specifically entropy and trace, yield insight into the representations learned by a neural network and how these can be improved through architecture scaling. These results are demonstrated first on test cases before being shown on more complex networks, including transformers, auto-encoders, graph neural networks, and reinforcement learning studies. In testing on a wide range of architectures, we highlight the universal nature of training dynamics and further discuss how it can be used to understand the mechanisms behind learning in neural networks. We identify two such dominant mechanisms present throughout machine learning training. The first, information compression, is seen through a reduction in the entropy of the NTK spectrum during training, and occurs predominantly in small neural networks. The second, coined structure formation, is seen through an increasing entropy and thus, the creation of structure in the neural network representations beyond the prior established by the network at initialization. Due to the ubiquity of the latter in deep neural network architectures and its flexibility in the creation of feature-rich representations, we argue that this form of evolution of the network's entropy be considered the onset of a deep learning regime.

papers.title: The Cognitive Revolution in Interpretability: From Explaining Behavior to Interpreting Representations and Algorithms
papers.research_question: How can we understand, interpret, and explain the behavior of complex intelligent AI systems like large language models, and how can mechanistic interpretability be grounded in cognitive science?
papers.core_contribution: The paper grounds mechanistic interpretability in cognitive science, proposing a taxonomy that categorizes interpretation methods into semantic interpretation (what latent representations are learned) and algorithmic interpretation (what operations are performed over representations).
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that a cognitive revolution in deep learning interpretability is underway, shifting from explaining behavior to interpreting representations and algorithms, and calls for a unified framework that integrates semantic and algorithmic interpretation.
papers.key_findings:
Current interpretability methods are ripe for a transition echoing the 'cognitive revolution' in psychology, shifting from pure behaviorism to studying internal representations and processing.
A taxonomy mirroring computational neuroscience distinguishes semantic interpretation (studying latent representations) and algorithmic interpretation (studying operations and algorithms).
Semantic interpretation methods include optimization and search, structural probing, causal probing, and dictionary learning, each with distinct assumptions and challenges.
Algorithmic interpretation focuses on circuit discovery, using interventions like knockouts and patching to understand the role of sub-networks in model behavior.
The paper discusses parallels and distinctions between approaches, analyzes strengths and weaknesses, and outlines challenges and the possibility of a unified framework.
future_direction: Unifying semantic and algorithmic interpretation under a common framework.
Addressing challenges in scalability, evaluation, and the Rashomon effect in causal analysis.
Developing automated and scalable methods for feature interpretation and evaluation in dictionary learning.
papers.abstract: Artificial neural networks have long been understood as "black boxes": though we know their computation graphs and learned parameters, the knowledge encoded by these weights and functions they perform are not inherently interpretable. As such, from the early days of deep learning, there have been efforts to explain these models' behavior and understand them internally; and recently, mechanistic interpretability (MI) has emerged as a distinct research area studying the features and implicit algorithms learned by foundation models such as large language models. In this work, we aim to ground MI in the context of cognitive science, which has long struggled with analogous questions in studying and explaining the behavior of "black box" intelligent systems like the human brain. We leverage several important ideas and developments in the history of cognitive science to disentangle divergent objectives in MI and indicate a clear path forward. First, we argue that current methods are ripe to facilitate a transition in deep learning interpretation echoing the "cognitive revolution" in 20th-century psychology that shifted the study of human psychology from pure behaviorism toward mental representations and processing. Second, we propose a taxonomy mirroring key parallels in computational neuroscience to describe two broad categories of MI research, semantic interpretation (what latent representations are learned and used) and algorithmic interpretation (what operations are performed over representations) to elucidate their divergent goals and objects of study. Finally, we elaborate the parallels and distinctions between various approaches in both categories, analyze the respective strengths and weaknesses of representative works, clarify underlying assumptions, outline key challenges, and discuss the possibility of unifying these modes of interpretation under a common framework.

papers.title: Questioning Representational Optimism in Deep Learning: The Fractured Entangled Representation Hypothesis
papers.research_question: Does better performance necessarily imply better internal representations? This paper challenges the view of representational optimism by comparing the internal representations of networks trained via open-ended search versus conventional stochastic gradient descent (SGD).
papers.core_contribution: The paper challenges representational optimism by introducing the Fractured Entangled Representation (FER) hypothesis, demonstrating that networks trained with conventional SGD can develop disorganized internal representations (FER) even when output performance is good, whereas networks from open-ended search can achieve more organized Unified Factored Representations (UFR).
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that Fractured Entangled Representation (FER) is a potential issue in conventional deep learning, raising questions about the adaptability of models trained via SGD, and that understanding and mitigating FER could be critical for the future of representation learning.
papers.key_findings:
Networks trained with conventional SGD to produce a target image exhibit Fractured Entangled Representations (FER), where information for unitary concepts is split into disconnected, redundant pieces that become entangled.
Networks evolved through the open-ended Picbreeder process for the same output image exhibit Unified Factored Representations (UFR), where concepts are represented in a single, modular, and reusable manner.
Weight sweeps reveal that UFR networks allow for meaningful, human-recognizable variations (e.g., changing symmetry, stem angle) while respecting regularities, whereas FER networks produce deleterious, entangled changes that break regularities.
The path (curriculum) taken during learning influences the final representation; open-ended search discovers fundamental regularities (like symmetry) early, which are then elaborated upon, while conventional SGD takes a direct, greedy path.
The paper speculates that FER in large models may underlie challenges in generalization, creativity, and continual learning, and that the order in which concepts are learned is fundamental to the quality of the internal representation.
papers.limitation:
The study is conducted on a minimal, toy task (generating a single image) using CPPNs/MLPs, which is far simpler than large-scale models like LLMs.
The implications of FER for large models are speculative and based on analogy and limited examples of LLM behavior.
future_direction: Investigate FER in large models like LLMs and explore ways to mitigate it.
Study the impact of curricula and the ordering of concepts during training on the development of FER/UFR.
Explore alternative training algorithms and objectives (e.g., open-ended, novelty-seeking) that might lead to better internal representations.
papers.abstract: Much of the excitement in modern AI is driven by the observation that scaling up existing systems leads to better performance. But does better performance necessarily imply better internal representations? While the representational optimist assumes it must, this position paper challenges that view. We compare neural networks evolved through an open-ended search process to networks trained via conventional stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on the simple task of generating a single image. This minimal setup offers a unique advantage: each hidden neuron's full functional behavior can be easily visualized as an image, thus revealing how the network's output behavior is internally constructed neuron by neuron. The result is striking: while both networks produce the same output behavior, their internal representations differ dramatically. The SGD-trained networks exhibit a form of disorganization that we term fractured entangled representation (FER). Interestingly, the evolved networks largely lack FER, even approaching a unified factored representation (UFR). In large models, FER may be degrading core model capacities like generalization, creativity, and (continual) learning. Therefore, understanding and mitigating FER could be critical to the future of representation learning.

papers.title: Letters of the Alphabet: Discovering Natural Feature Sets
papers.research_question: How do hidden layers in a simple neural network represent input features, and how can natural feature sets be derived from the data?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates how hidden node activations in a neural network can be visualized to understand feature representation and how natural feature sets can be discovered by grouping similar inputs.
papers.conclusion: The experiments provide a step-by-step blueprint for how neural networks derive natural feature sets from data, offering insights into feature representation in hidden layers.
papers.key_findings:
Hidden nodes in the network activate to specific features like vertical and horizontal bars in letter representations.
Nodes 2 and 5 are activated strongly by most letters, indicating potential overfitting or redundancy.
Natural feature sets group similarly shaped letters, such as A and H, or B, R, and P.
Adding 10% noise did not improve generalization in the natural feature sets experiment.
Heatmap visualizations effectively show which input patterns contribute to hidden node activations.
papers.limitation:
Adding 10% noise did not help the hidden nodes generalize better as expected.
Deciphering and visualizing hidden node activations took a lot of time and explanation.
future_direction: Spend more time formatting visualizations to efficiently display hidden node activations for natural feature sets.
Use algorithms to automatically determine the ideal number of hidden nodes to speed up development.
papers.abstract: Deep learning networks find intricate features in large datasets using the backpropagation algorithm. This algorithm repeatedly adjusts the network connections.' weights and examining the "hidden" nodes behavior between the input and output layer provides better insight into how neural networks create feature representations. Experiments built on each other show that activity differences computed within a layer can guide learning. A simple neural network is used, which includes a data set comprised of the alphabet letters, where each letter forms 81 input nodes comprised of 0 and 1s and a single hidden layer and an output layer. The first experiment explains how the hidden layers in this simple neural network represent the input data's features. The second experiment attempts to reverse-engineer the neural network to find the alphabet's natural feature sets. As the network interprets features, we can understand how it derives the natural feature sets for a given data. This understanding is essential to delve deeper into deep generative models, such as Boltzmann machines. Deep generative models are a class of unsupervised deep learning algorithms. The primary function of deep generative models is to find the natural feature sets for a given data set.

papers.title: DistillLens: Symmetric Knowledge Distillation Through Logit Lens
papers.research_question: How can we improve knowledge distillation by aligning the intermediate thought processes of student and teacher models using symmetric divergence objectives?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DISTILLLENS, a knowledge distillation framework that uses Logit Lens and symmetric divergence to align intermediate layer distributions, improving student performance.
papers.conclusion: DISTILLLENS effectively aligns intermediate thought trajectories of student and teacher models, consistently outperforming standard KD and feature-transfer methods across GPT-2 and Llama architectures.
papers.key_findings:
DISTILLLENS outperforms standard KD and feature-transfer baselines on diverse instruction-following benchmarks.
The symmetric divergence objective (JSD) enforces a dual-sided penalty that prevents both overconfidence and underconfidence.
DISTILLLENS reduces exposure bias compared to standard KD without the computational overhead of on-policy methods.
The method is modular and can be combined with existing KD baselines, with the most improvement when combined with mode-seeking objectives like RKL.
Ablation studies show that using 5 interleaved intermediate layers yields the best performance.
papers.limitation: Computational overhead during training due to projecting multiple intermediate layers through the unembedding matrix.
future_direction: Inject complex reasoning capabilities into smaller architectures
Extend to cross-architecture distillation
papers.abstract: Standard Knowledge Distillation (KD) compresses Large Language Models (LLMs) by optimizing final outputs, yet it typically treats the teacher's intermediate layer's thought process as a black box. While feature-based distillation attempts to bridge this gap, existing methods (e.g., MSE and asymmetric KL divergence) ignore the rich uncertainty profiles required for the final output. In this paper, we introduce DistillLens, a framework that symmetrically aligns the evolving thought processes of student and teacher models. By projecting intermediate hidden states into the vocabulary space via the Logit Lens, we enforce structural alignment using a symmetric divergence objective. Our analysis proves that this constraint imposes a dual-sided penalty, preventing both overconfidence and underconfidence while preserving the high-entropy information conduits essential for final deduction. Extensive experiments on GPT-2 and Llama architectures demonstrate that DistillLens consistently outperforms standard KD and feature-transfer baselines on diverse instruction-following benchmarks. The code is available at https://github.com/manishdhakal/DistillLens.

papers.title: Transformer Language Models without Positional Encodings Still Learn Positional Information
papers.research_question: Can transformer language models learn positional information without explicit positional encodings, and how do they do it?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer language models without explicit positional encodings (NoPos) can learn implicit positional information and achieve competitive performance, and this ability is due to the causal attention mask.
papers.conclusion: Transformer language models can learn positional information without explicit encodings, and this phenomenon is robust across settings but does not extend to masked language models, with the causal attention mechanism being the key factor.
papers.key_findings:
NoPos models achieve competitive perplexity compared to models with explicit positional encodings across different datasets, model sizes, and sequence lengths.
Probing experiments show that NoPos models learn an implicit notion of absolute positions in their hidden representations, similar to models with learned positional embeddings.
The success of NoPos models is unique to causal language models; masked language models fail to converge without positional encodings.
Shuffling the prefix tokens leads to a dramatic increase in loss, indicating that the model uses the learned positional information.
The causal attention mask is conjectured to allow the model to infer absolute positions by counting the number of attendable tokens.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to models up to 1.3B parameters, and while the trend suggests the findings should hold for larger models, this is not tested.
NoPos models are always slightly worse than models with positional encodings, indicating that the inductive bias of positional encoding is important.
papers.abstract: Causal transformer language models (LMs), such as GPT-3, typically require some form of positional encoding, such as positional embeddings. However, we show that LMs without any explicit positional encoding are still competitive with standard models and that this phenomenon is robust across different datasets, model sizes, and sequence lengths.Probing experiments reveal that such models acquire an implicit notion of absolute positions throughout the network, effectively compensating for the missing information.We conjecture that causal attention enables the model to infer the number of predecessors that each token can attend to, thereby approximating its absolute position.Our findings indicate that causal LMs might derive positional awareness not only from the explicit positioning mechanism but also from the effects of the causal mask.

papers.title: Towards eliciting latent knowledge from LLMs with mechanistic interpretability
papers.research_question: How effective are mechanistic interpretability techniques (like Logit Lens and sparse autoencoders) at eliciting hidden knowledge from language models trained to conceal a secret?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Taboo model organism, a language model fine-tuned to hide a secret word, and demonstrates that mechanistic interpretability techniques (Logit Lens and sparse autoencoders) can be used to elicit this hidden knowledge.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability-based approaches show promise for eliciting hidden knowledge from LLMs, and the Taboo model provides a useful benchmark for future work on more complex forms of concealed information.
papers.key_findings:
The Taboo model successfully conceals its secret word, resisting direct and adversarial prompting.
Mechanistic interpretability methods (Logit Lens and SAEs) can elicit the secret word from the model's internal representations.
Token forcing is highly effective after the model is 'warmed up' with several turns of gameplay.
A separate LLM (Gemma 3) can guess the secret from the Taboo model's hints, confirming the hints are meaningful.
No evaluated method achieved perfect accuracy, indicating room for improvement in elicitation techniques.
papers.limitation:
The model organism uses a single-token secret word, representing a relatively simple form of hidden knowledge.
No evaluated method achieved near-perfect accuracy, even in this simplified setting.
future_direction: Explore more complex model organisms designed to hide multi-token secrets, abstract concepts, or hidden objectives.
papers.abstract: As language models become more powerful and sophisticated, it is crucial that they remain trustworthy and reliable. There is concerning preliminary evidence that models may attempt to deceive or keep secrets from their operators. To explore the ability of current techniques to elicit such hidden knowledge, we train a Taboo model: a language model that describes a specific secret word without explicitly stating it. Importantly, the secret word is not presented to the model in its training data or prompt. We then investigate methods to uncover this secret. First, we evaluate non-interpretability (black-box) approaches. Subsequently, we develop largely automated strategies based on mechanistic interpretability techniques, including logit lens and sparse autoencoders. Evaluation shows that both approaches are effective in eliciting the secret word in our proof-of-concept setting. Our findings highlight the promise of these approaches for eliciting hidden knowledge and suggest several promising avenues for future work, including testing and refining these methods on more complex model organisms. This work aims to be a step towards addressing the crucial problem of eliciting secret knowledge from language models, thereby contributing to their safe and reliable deployment.

papers.title: ERNIE-Tiny : A Progressive Distillation Framework for Pretrained Transformer Compression
papers.research_question: How to effectively compress pretrained language models (PLMs) by addressing the pretrain-finetune distillation discrepancy through a smooth transition of teacher, training data, and learning objective?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a four-stage progressive distillation framework (ERNIE-Tiny) that smooths the transition from pretrain to finetune distillation by gradually altering teacher model, training data, and learning objective, introducing a novel general-enhanced distillation stage to improve student generalization.
papers.conclusion: The proposed progressive distillation framework ERNIE-Tiny effectively compresses pretrained language models, maintaining high performance while significantly reducing model size and inference time, and demonstrates improved generalization.
papers.key_findings:
A 4-layer ERNIE-Tiny student maintains over 98% of its 12-layer teacher BERTbase performance on the GLUE benchmark with 9.4x faster inference speed.
The general-enhanced distillation stage, which uses a finetuned teacher on general data, improves the student model's generalization, especially on low-resource tasks.
The task-adaptive distillation stage serves as a crucial bridge, smoothing the transition between general and task-specific data distillation and improving final performance.
ERNIE-Tiny achieves state-of-the-art compression results on both English (GLUE) and Chinese NLP tasks, outperforming the teacher BERTbase on Chinese tasks with 7.5x fewer parameters.
Ablation studies confirm the importance of each distillation stage, with the removal of any stage leading to performance degradation.
papers.limitation: The work did not apply larger unlabeled general data such as C4, leaving more efficient data utilization for future work.
future_direction: Applying larger unlabeled general data (e.g., C4) and exploring more efficient data utilization.
papers.abstract: Pretrained language models (PLMs) such as BERT adopt a training paradigm which first pretrain the model in general data and then finetune the model on task-specific data, and have recently achieved great success. However, PLMs are notorious for their enormous parameters and hard to be deployed on real-life applications. Knowledge distillation has been prevailing to address this problem by transferring knowledge from a large teacher to a much smaller student over a set of data.
