We argue that the selection of thee three key components, namely teacher, training data, and learning objective, is crucial to the effectiveness of distillation. We, therefore, propose a four-stage progressive distillation framework ERNIE-Tiny to compress PLM, which varies the three components gradually from general level to task-specific level. Specifically, the first stage, General Distillation, performs distillation with guidance from pretrained teacher, gerenal data and latent distillation loss. Then, General-Enhanced Distillation changes teacher model from pretrained teacher to finetuned teacher. After that, Task-Adaptive Distillation shifts training data from general data to task-specific data. In the end, Task-Specific Distillation, adds two additional losses, namely Soft-Label and Hard-Label loss onto the last stage. Empirical results demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework and generalization gain brought by ERNIE-Tiny.In particular, experiments show that a 4-layer ERNIE-Tiny maintains over 98.0%performance of its 12-layer teacher BERT base on GLUE benchmark, surpassing state-of-the-art (SOTA) by 1.0% GLUE score with the same amount of parameters. Moreover, ERNIE-Tiny achieves a new compression SOTA on five Chinese NLP tasks, outperforming BERT base by 0.4% accuracy with 7.5x fewer parameters and9.4x faster inference speed.

papers.title: Understanding trained CNNs by indexing neuron selectivity
papers.research_question: How can we understand and visualize the internal representations of Convolutional Neural Networks by indexing neuron selectivity to specific properties like color and class?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework to understand CNN internal representations by visualizing Neuron Features and quantifying neuron selectivity indexes for color and class, enabling the analysis of how features and classes are represented across layers.
papers.conclusion: The framework successfully indexes neuron selectivity, showing how color and class representations are organized across CNN layers, with implications for understanding neural coding principles.
papers.key_findings:
Color selectivity is present in all convolutional layers, with 40% in conv1 and 30% in conv2, decreasing but still present in deeper layers.
Class selectivity increases with depth, with over 50% of neurons in conv5 having high class selectivity (index >0.6).
Neuron Feature visualization reveals clear shapes for some neurons and blurred features for others, suggesting different coding strategies.
The framework can identify specific neurons selective to colors or classes, such as a red-mushroom neuron in conv4 or dog-face neurons in conv5.
Color is important for object recognition, as grayscale images lead to higher classification errors.
future_direction: Apply indexes to different neural network architectures.
Define new selectivity indexes for shape, texture, or part detection.
Study relations between indexes.

papers.title: Half-Space Feature Learning in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How do neural networks learn features? The paper investigates whether neural networks learn simple half-space features and how gradient descent allocates resources (paths) to different regions of the input space.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Deep Linearly Gated Network (DLGN), a model that learns simple half-space features, and shows that feature learning in neural networks involves gradient descent allocating more paths to easier regions of the input space.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that neural networks learn simple half-space features, and that gradient descent allocates more resources to easier regions, which can be visualized in DLGNs, providing enhanced interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
DLGNs can perform comparably to ReLU networks on datasets like CIFAR-10 while being more interpretable.
Feature learning in neural networks involves changes in the active path regions, which can be tracked via the overlap kernel.
Gradient descent tends to allocate more paths (resources) to regions of the input space where the target function is simpler (lower frequency).
The empirical NTK changes during training to become better suited to the task, and this change is driven by the evolution of active path regions.
In DLGNs, neurons in later layers tend to specialize to simpler regions (e.g., half-spaces) that cover low-frequency parts of the target function.
papers.limitation: Analysis of ReLU networks is complicated due to their complex path active regions, so the study uses DLGNs as a surrogate.
future_direction: Investigating defects of gradient descent in resource allocation and developing architecture-aware optimization algorithms.
Further study of the phenomenon of neurons focusing on easy regions.
papers.abstract: There currently exist two extreme viewpoints for neural network feature learning -- (i) Neural networks simply implement a kernel method (a la NTK) and hence no features are learned (ii) Neural networks can represent (and hence learn) intricate hierarchical features suitable for the data. We argue in this paper neither interpretation is likely to be correct based on a novel viewpoint. Neural networks can be viewed as a mixture of experts, where each expert corresponds to a (number of layers length) path through a sequence of hidden units. We use this alternate interpretation to motivate a model, called the Deep Linearly Gated Network (DLGN), which sits midway between deep linear networks and ReLU networks. Unlike deep linear networks, the DLGN is capable of learning non-linear features (which are then linearly combined), and unlike ReLU networks these features are ultimately simple -- each feature is effectively an indicator function for a region compactly described as an intersection of (number of layers) half-spaces in the input space. This viewpoint allows for a comprehensive global visualization of features, unlike the local visualizations for neurons based on saliency/activation/gradient maps. Feature learning in DLGNs is shown to happen and the mechanism with which this happens is through learning half-spaces in the input space that contain smooth regions of the target function. Due to the structure of DLGNs, the neurons in later layers are fundamentally the same as those in earlier layers -- they all represent a half-space -- however, the dynamics of gradient descent impart a distinct clustering to the later layer neurons. We hypothesize that ReLU networks also have similar feature learning behaviour.

papers.title: Feature Integration Spaces: Joint Training Reveals Dual Encoding in Neural Network Representations
papers.research_question: Does neural network encode information in two complementary spaces: feature identity and feature integration?
papers.core_contribution: This work provides systematic evidence for dual encoding in neural representations, meaningful nonlinearly encoded feature integrations, and introduces an architectural paradigm shift from post-hoc feature analysis to integrated computational design.
papers.conclusion: This work provides the first systematic evidence for dual-encoding spaces in neural network representations and introduces an architectural solution that achieves substantial improvements across multiple validation metrics, establishing foundations for next-generation SAEs.
papers.key_findings:
Joint training achieves 41.3% reconstruction improvement and 51.6% reduction in KL divergence errors over SAE-only baseline.
The architecture spontaneously develops bimodal feature organization with low squared norm features specializing in integration pathways.
Integration features exhibit selective sensitivity to experimental manipulations and produce statistically significant nonlinear interaction effects on model outputs.
Nonlinear integration components achieve 16.5% standalone improvement using only 3% of parameters, demonstrating parameter efficiency.
Sequential SAE+NFM approach shows 23.4% error reduction and 29.8% reduction in pathological KL divergence errors.
papers.limitation:
Scale constraints represent one primary limitation of this work. Our experiments on a 3B parameter model with 50k SAE features provide proof-of-concept evidence, but scaling to industrial-scale models with millions of features is likely challenging.
Integration interpretability presents ongoing challenges. While we demonstrated functional effects, these features remain largely opaque to direct inspection.
Limitations of traditional feature discovery approaches, as maximum activation analysis on secondary features failed to yield interpretable patterns.
future_direction: Dynamic analysis of how integration patterns evolve during training
Cross-model validation
Cross-layer analysis
papers.abstract: Current sparse autoencoder (SAE) approaches to neural network interpretability assume that activations can be decomposed through linear superposition into sparse, interpretable features. Despite high reconstruction fidelity, SAEs consistently fail to eliminate polysemanticity and exhibit pathological behavioral errors. We propose that neural networks encode information in two complementary spaces compressed into the same substrate: feature identity and feature integration. To test this dual encoding hypothesis, we develop sequential and joint-training architectures to capture identity and integration patterns simultaneously. Joint training achieves 41.3% reconstruction improvement and 51.6% reduction in KL divergence errors. This architecture spontaneously develops bimodal feature organization: low squared norm features contributing to integration pathways and the rest contributing directly to the residual. Small nonlinear components (3% of parameters) achieve 16.5% standalone improvements, demonstrating parameter-efficient capture of computational relationships crucial for behavior. Additionally, intervention experiments using 2x2 factorial stimulus designs demonstrated that integration features exhibit selective sensitivity to experimental manipulations and produce systematic behavioral effects on model outputs, including significant statistical interaction effects across semantic dimensions. This work provides systematic evidence for (1) dual encoding in neural representations, (2) meaningful nonlinearly encoded feature interactions, and (3) introduces an architectural paradigm shift from post-hoc feature analysis to integrated computational design, establishing foundations for next-generation SAEs.

papers.title: Beyond Distribution Shift: Spurious Features Through the Lens of Training Dynamics
papers.research_question: How do spurious features affect model generalization, and can harmful spurious features be detected early during training by monitoring training dynamics?
papers.core_contribution: Spurious features can be benign or harmful depending on whether they are harder or easier to learn than core features. Harmful spurious features can be detected early by monitoring training dynamics using instance difficulty metrics like Prediction Depth.
papers.conclusion: Monitoring early training dynamics using suitable instance difficulty metrics can help identify harmful spurious features, saving time and computational costs and aiding in developing reliable models.
papers.key_findings:
Not all spurious features are harmful; they are harmful only if they are easier to learn than core features.
Prediction Depth (PD) can quantify feature difficulty and identify harmful spurious features during training.
Harmful spurious features can be detected by observing the learning dynamics of a DNN's early layers.
Monitoring only accuracy during training is insufficient to detect spurious features; instance difficulty metrics are needed.
Theoretical connections exist between Prediction Depth and information-theoretic concepts like V-usable information.
future_direction: Develop intervention schemes to fix spurious feature problems early.
Unlearning spurious features from model representations.
papers.abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are prone to learning spurious features that correlate with the label during training but are irrelevant to the learning problem. This hurts model generalization and poses problems when deploying them in safety-critical applications. This paper aims to better understand the effects of spurious features through the lens of the learning dynamics of the internal neurons during the training process. We make the following observations: (1) While previous works highlight the harmful effects of spurious features on the generalization ability of DNNs, we emphasize that not all spurious features are harmful. Spurious features can be "benign" or "harmful" depending on whether they are "harder" or "easier" to learn than the core features for a given model. This definition is model and dataset dependent. (2) We build upon this premise and use instance difficulty methods (like Prediction Depth (Baldock et al., 2021)) to quantify "easiness" for a given model and to identify this behavior during the training phase. (3) We empirically show that the harmful spurious features can be detected by observing the learning dynamics of the DNN's early layers. In other words, easy features learned by the initial layers of a DNN early during the training can (potentially) hurt model generalization. We verify our claims on medical and vision datasets, both simulated and real, and justify the empirical success of our hypothesis by showing the theoretical connections between Prediction Depth and information-theoretic concepts like 𝒱-usable information (Ethayarajh et al., 2021). Lastly, our experiments show that monitoring only accuracy during training (as is common in machine learning pipelines) is insufficient to detect spurious features. We, therefore, highlight the need for monitoring early training dynamics using suitable instance difficulty metrics.

papers.title: The Low-Dimensional Linear Geometry of Contextualized Word Representations
papers.research_question: How are linguistic features encoded in the linear geometry of contextualized word representations, and what are the geometric properties of these encodings?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that linguistic features are encoded in low-dimensional linear subspaces of contextualized word representations, that these subspaces have hierarchical structure and are distributed across neurons, and that they are causally relevant to model behavior.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a probing procedure that reveals low-dimensional linear subspaces encoding linguistic features in word representations, with hierarchical and distributed structure, and shows these subspaces are causally relevant to model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Linguistic features are encoded in low-dimensional subspaces of contextualized word representations.
These subspaces exhibit hierarchical structure (e.g., noun and verb subspaces nested within part-of-speech subspaces).
The subspaces are distributed across neurons rather than aligned with individual axes.
Ablating specific subspaces (e.g., nounspace or verbspace) impairs BERT's performance on subject-verb agreement, indicating causal relevance.
Contextual representations encode linguistic variables better but not more compactly than non-contextual word embeddings.
future_direction: Explore richer geometric structure in word representations and its effect on model behavior.
papers.abstract: Black-box probing models can reliably extract linguistic features like tense, number, and syntactic role from pretrained word representations. However, the manner in which these features are encoded in representations remains poorly understood. We present a systematic study of the linear geometry of contextualized word representations in ELMO and BERT. We show that a variety of linguistic features (including structured dependency relationships) are encoded in low-dimensional subspaces. We then refine this geometric picture, showing that there are hierarchical relations between the subspaces encoding general linguistic categories and more specific ones, and that lowdimensional feature encodings are distributed rather than aligned to individual neurons. Finally, we demonstrate that these linear subspaces are causally related to model behavior, and can be used to perform fine-grained manipulation of BERT's output distribution.

papers.title: MoEfication: Transformer Feed-forward Layers are Mixtures of Experts
papers.research_question: Do functional partitions emerge in feed-forward networks (FFNs) of pre-trained Transformers, similar to mixtures of experts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that feed-forward networks in Transformers are naturally mixtures of experts and introduces MoEfication, a method to convert standard models into MoE versions, enabling efficient inference with minimal performance loss.
papers.conclusion: The work verifies that Transformer FFNs are mixtures of experts and that MoEfication can convert models to MoE versions for efficient inference and provide insights into FFN mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
FFNs in pre-trained Transformers exhibit sparse activation, with most inputs activating only a tiny fraction of neurons.
MoEfication can maintain over 95% of original performance while using only 10-30% of FFN parameters.
MoEfication significantly reduces inference FLOPS, achieving up to 2x speedup with 25% of FFN parameters.
Routing patterns in MoEfied models reveal both general experts (used for most inputs) and input-specific experts (seldom used).
Larger models have sparser activations, making MoEfication more effective for them.
future_direction: Explaining the sparse activation phenomenon empirically or theoretically.
Inspiring future work on the design and training of MoE models.
papers.abstract: Recent work has shown that feed-forward networks (FFNs) in pre-trained Transformers are a key component, storing various linguistic and factual knowledge. However, the computational patterns of FFNs are still unclear. In this work, we study the computational patterns of FFNs and observe that most inputs only activate a tiny ratio of neurons of FFNs. This phenomenon is similar to the sparsity of the human brain, which drives research on functional partitions of the human brain. To verify whether functional partitions also emerge in FFNs, we propose to convert a model into its MoE version with the same parameters, namely MoEfication. Specifically, MoEfication consists of two phases: (1) splitting the parameters of FFNs into multiple functional partitions as experts, and (2) building expert routers to decide which experts will be used for each input. Experimental results show that MoEfication can conditionally use 10% to 30% of FFN parameters while maintaining over 95% original performance for different models on various downstream tasks. Besides, MoEfication brings two advantages: (1) it significantly reduces the FLOPS of inference, i.e., 2x speedup with 25% of FFN parameters, and (2) it provides a fine-grained perspective to study the inner mechanism of FFNs. The source code of this paper can be obtained from https://github.com/ thunlp/MoEfication.

papers.title: Inspecting and Editing Knowledge Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we map natural language statements to fact encodings in an LM's internal representations to enable editing and probing of knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: REMEDI is a method that learns to map natural language statements to fact encodings in LM representations, enabling both editing of knowledge (by adding vectors to hidden representations) and probing of existing knowledge.
papers.conclusion: REMEDI links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.
papers.key_findings:
REMEDI can patch errors made by an LM and insert new facts with or without context provided in the prompt.
REMEDI can help detect errors before generation by comparing edit vectors to unedited representations.
REMEDI increases accuracy on occupation classification and factual editing tasks compared to prompting baselines.
REMEDI generalizes from out-of-context training to in-context editing, suggesting unified representation of background and contextual knowledge.
REMEDI edits preserve correlations between features (e.g., adding 'made of metal' increases probability of 'shiny').
papers.limitation:
REMEDI can occasionally lead to disfluent or incorrect generations.
REMEDI sometimes damages the essence of the entity (e.g., making Wiener schnitzel an anime instead of a food).
REMEDI can also cause unrelated facts to change (e.g., changing the air dates of a TV show).
future_direction: Developing controlled generation interfaces that allow direct steering of model behavior in representation space.
Building tools for monitoring and controlling language generation by directly specifying facts and situations in an LM's native encoding scheme.
papers.abstract: Neural language models (LMs) represent facts about the world described by text. Sometimes these facts derive from training data (in most LMs, a representation of the word "banana" encodes the fact that bananas are fruits). Sometimes facts derive from input text itself (a representation of the sentence "I poured out the bottle" encodes the fact that the bottle became empty). We describe REMEDI, a method for learning to map statements in natural language to fact encodings in an LM's internal representation system. REMEDI encodings can be used as knowledge editors: when added to LM hidden representations, they modify downstream generation to be consistent with new facts. REMEDI encodings may also be used as probes: when compared to LM representations, they reveal which properties LMs already attribute to mentioned entities, in some cases making it possible to predict when LMs will generate outputs that conflict with background knowledge or input text. REMEDI thus links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.

papers.title: Exploring explicit coarse-grained structure in artificial neural networks
papers.research_question: How can hierarchical coarse-grained structure be explicitly employed in neural networks to improve interpretability without degrading performance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces hierarchical coarse-grained structure into neural networks to improve interpretability without degrading performance, via TaylorNet for classification and a multi-level data distillation setup.
papers.conclusion: The hierarchical coarse-grained structure improves interpretability without degrading performance, and TaylorNet and the distillation setup are effective.
papers.key_findings:
TaylorNet achieves 99.2% accuracy on MNIST and 71.7% on CIFAR-10 with fewer parameters than some baseline models.
Coarse-grained operations in TaylorNet are more powerful than convolution operations for representing nonlinear mappings.
The multi-level data distillation process captures essential features of the dataset, and distilled images can be used as references for classification.
Weight distribution analysis shows that dominant terms in Taylor expansion are local.
The hierarchical coarse-grained structure makes neural networks more understandable while maintaining acceptable performance.
papers.limitation:
The loss function in distillation could be designed more smartly.
The partition of the dataset and choice of hyperparameter λ might affect the distillation results.
The fixed point of the scale transformations is not discussed.
future_direction: Using multiple TaylorNets with orthogonality constraints for higher efficiency.
Studying fixed points of scale transformations in TaylorNet and the iterative distillation procedure.
papers.abstract: We propose to employ the hierarchical coarse-grained structure in the artificial neural networks explicitly to improve the interpretability without degrading performance. The idea has been applied in two situations. One is a neural network called TaylorNet, which aims to approximate the general mapping from input data to output result in terms of Taylor series directly, without resorting to any magic nonlinear activations. The other is a new setup for data distillation, which can perform multi-level abstraction of the input dataset and generate new data that possesses the relevant features of the original dataset and can be used as references for classification. In both cases, the coarse-grained structure plays an important role in simplifying the network and improving both the interpretability and efficiency. The validity has been demonstrated on MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets. Further improvement and some open questions related are also discussed.

papers.title: Towards Interpretable Deep Neural Networks by Leveraging Adversarial Examples
papers.research_question: What do neurons in deep neural networks truly detect, and are deep visual representations robust distributed codes of visual concepts? The paper investigates these questions using adversarial examples.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that neurons in DNNs are not true object detectors but respond to discriminative patches, and deep visual representations are not robust. It then proposes an adversarial training scheme with a consistent loss to improve interpretability and consistency of representations.
papers.conclusion: Adversarial training with a consistent loss improves the interpretability and robustness of DNNs, allowing human users to understand model predictions and errors through interpretable representations.
papers.key_findings:
Neurons in DNNs do not truly detect semantic objects/parts but respond to objects/parts as recurrent discriminative patches.
Deep visual representations are not robust distributed codes of visual concepts because representations of adversarial images are inconsistent with those of real images.
Adversarial training with a consistent loss improves interpretability, making neurons detect true objects/parts and representations more consistent.
Interpretable representations enable tracing predictions back to influential neurons, explaining how models make predictions and errors.
Adversarial training also improves model robustness against adversarial attacks.
papers.limitation: Adversarial training causes a drop in accuracy on real images, representing a trade-off between performance and interpretability/robustness.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have demonstrated impressive performance on a wide array of tasks, but they are usually considered opaque since internal structure and learned parameters are not interpretable. In this paper, we re-examine the internal representations of DNNs using adversarial images, which are generated by an ensemble-optimization algorithm. We find that: (1) the neurons in DNNs do not truly detect semantic objects/parts, but respond to objects/parts only as recurrent discriminative patches; (2) deep visual representations are not robust distributed codes of visual concepts because the representations of adversarial images are largely not consistent with those of real images, although they have similar visual appearance, both of which are different from previous findings. To further improve the interpretability of DNNs, we propose an adversarial training scheme with a consistent loss such that the neurons are endowed with human-interpretable concepts. The induced interpretable representations enable us to trace eventual outcomes back to influential neurons. Therefore, human users can know how the models make predictions, as well as when and why they make errors.

papers.title: Shape or Texture: Understanding Discriminative Features in CNNs
papers.research_question: What type of shape information is discriminative in CNNs, where is shape information encoded, and when does the network learn about object shape during training?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that CNNs learn shape information early in training, encode it primarily in the last few layers, and that shape encoding does not guarantee per-pixel semantic understanding.
papers.conclusion: The paper provides a systematic study of shape encoding in CNNs, revealing important mechanisms that characterize a network's ability to encode shape information, which can inform the design of more robust and trustworthy computer vision algorithms.
papers.key_findings:
CNNs learn the majority of shape information during the first few epochs of training.
Shape information is largely encoded in the last few layers of a CNN.
Biasing a CNN towards shape changes the number of shape encoding neurons in the last feature encoding stage.
Early layers also encode shape information, which can be combined with deeper layers for better shape extraction.
Encoding shape does not imply the encoding of localized per-pixel semantic information.
papers.abstract: Contrasting the previous evidence that neurons in the later layers of a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) respond to complex object shapes, recent studies have shown that CNNs actually exhibit a `texture bias': given an image with both texture and shape cues (e.g., a stylized image), a CNN is biased towards predicting the category corresponding to the texture. However, these previous studies conduct experiments on the final classification output of the network, and fail to robustly evaluate the bias contained (i) in the latent representations, and (ii) on a per-pixel level. In this paper, we design a series of experiments that overcome these issues. We do this with the goal of better understanding what type of shape information contained in the network is discriminative, where shape information is encoded, as well as when the network learns about object shape during training. We show that a network learns the majority of overall shape information at the first few epochs of training and that this information is largely encoded in the last few layers of a CNN. Finally, we show that the encoding of shape does not imply the encoding of localized per-pixel semantic information. The experimental results and findings provide a more accurate understanding of the behaviour of current CNNs, thus helping to inform future design choices.

papers.title: Convergent Learning: Do different neural networks learn the same representations?
papers.research_question: Do different neural networks with the same architecture trained from different random initializations learn the same representations (i.e., exhibit convergent learning)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces methods to compare neural network representations and shows that networks exhibit partial convergent learning, with some features learned reliably across networks and others not, and that representations are a mix of local and slightly distributed codes.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks exhibit convergent learning to some extent, and the introduced methods are effective for understanding and comparing the representations they learn.
papers.key_findings:
Some features are learned reliably in multiple networks, yet other features are not consistently learned.
Units learn to span low-dimensional subspaces and, while these subspaces are common to multiple networks, the specific basis vectors learned are not.
The representation codes show evidence of being a mix between a local (single unit) code and slightly, but not fully, distributed codes across multiple units.
The average activation values of neurons vary considerably within a network, yet the mean activation values across different networks converge to an almost identical distribution.
Features learned in different networks are most convergent on the first convolutional layer (conv1) and least convergent on the fourth (conv4).
papers.limitation: Mapping layers for higher layers (conv3-conv5) showed poor performance, and the reasons are not fully understood.
future_direction: Investigate different architectures, training algorithms, and hyperparameters.
Train more powerful predictive models for higher layers with different hyperparameters or architectures.
papers.abstract: Recent success in training deep neural networks have prompted active investigation into the features learned on their intermediate layers. Such research is difficult because it requires making sense of non-linear computations performed by millions of parameters, but valuable because it increases our ability to understand current models and create improved versions of them. In this paper we investigate the extent to which neural networks exhibit what we call convergent learning, which is when the representations learned by multiple nets converge to a set of features which are either individually similar between networks or where subsets of features span similar low-dimensional spaces. We propose a specific method of probing representations: training multiple networks and then comparing and contrasting their individual, learned representations at the level of neurons or groups of neurons. We begin research into this question using three techniques to approximately align different neural networks on a feature level: a bipartite matching approach that makes one-to-one assignments between neurons, a sparse prediction approach that finds one-to-many mappings, and a spectral clustering approach that finds many-to-many mappings. This initial investigation reveals a few previously unknown properties of neural networks, and we argue that future research into the question of convergent learning will yield many more. The insights described here include (1) that some features are learned reliably in multiple networks, yet other features are not consistently learned; (2) that units learn to span low-dimensional subspaces and, while these subspaces are common to multiple networks, the specific basis vectors learned are not; (3) that the representation codes show evidence of being a mix between a local code and slightly, but not fully, distributed codes across multiple units.

papers.title: On the Interplay Between Fine-tuning and Sentence-level Probing for Linguistic Knowledge in Pre-trained Transformers
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning affect the representations and linguistic knowledge in pre-trained transformer models, and to what extent can changes in probing accuracy be attributed to changes in linguistic knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that fine-tuning pre-trained transformer models affects sentence-level probing accuracy, but these changes are not straightforward and often not due to acquisition or loss of linguistic knowledge; instead, they can be attributed to changes in attention distribution or other factors, requiring careful interpretation.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that fine-tuning can lead to substantial changes in probing accuracy, but these changes require careful interpretation as they may not directly indicate changes in linguistic knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning affects probing accuracy, with changes typically larger for higher layers.
Changes in probing accuracy vary across models, fine-tuning tasks, and probing tasks.
Improvements in probing accuracy with CLS-pooling can be attributed to changes in attention distribution rather than acquisition of new linguistic knowledge.
Fine-tuning can negatively affect probing accuracy, possibly due to changes in representations.
Only in few cases does fine-tuning improve probing accuracy beyond using a strong pooling method like mean-pooling.
papers.limitation: It remains unclear whether fine-tuning indeed removes the linguistic knowledge or whether it is simply no longer linearly separable.
future_direction: Further investigation into whether fine-tuning removes linguistic knowledge or just makes it not linearly separable.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning pre-trained contextualized embedding models has become an integral part of the NLP pipeline. At the same time, probing has emerged as a way to investigate the linguistic knowledge captured by pre-trained models. Very little is, however, understood about how fine-tuning affects the representations of pre-trained models and thereby the linguistic knowledge they encode. This paper contributes towards closing this gap. We study three different pre-trained models: BERT, RoBERTa, and ALBERT, and investigate through sentence-level probing how finetuning affects their representations. We find that for some probing tasks fine-tuning leads to substantial changes in accuracy, possibly suggesting that fine-tuning introduces or even removes linguistic knowledge from a pre-trained model. These changes, however, vary greatly across different models, fine-tuning and probing tasks. Our analysis reveals that while finetuning indeed changes the representations of a pre-trained model and these changes are typically larger for higher layers, only in very few cases, fine-tuning has a positive effect on probing accuracy that is larger than just using the pre-trained model with a strong pooling method. Based on our findings, we argue that both positive and negative effects of finetuning on probing require a careful interpretation.

papers.title: From Passive to Persuasive: Steering Emotional Nuance in Human-AI Negotiation
papers.research_question: Whether complex social behaviors, such as empathy and strategic politeness, are encoded as localized, approximately linear directions in LLM activation space and can be effectively steered via attribution-guided activation injection.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces STAR, a two-stage inference-time framework that uses attribution patching to localize where behavioral traits causally originate and injects contrastive activation vectors at those positions. It demonstrates that complex interpersonal behaviors are encoded as localized, linear directions in activation space and can be effectively steered.
papers.conclusion: The findings indicate that complex interpersonal stances are recoverable as precise, localized directions in residual stream space, and that the central challenge in behavioral alignment is identifying where behavioral intent is encoded, not model capacity.
papers.key_findings:
Localized activation injection (STAR) consistently outperforms global steering and instruction priming across emotional dialogue and negotiation tasks.
Steering effects persist and can compound across multi-turn interactions, with larger effect sizes than in single-turn settings.
Human evaluation confirms that automatic metric gains reflect genuine improvements in perceived conversational quality, not superficial lexical changes.
Attribution patching reveals that behavioral traits localize to specific early-layer attention and MLP components, with distinct patterns for affective vs. strategic tasks.
The work challenges the assumption that complex, context-dependent social behaviors resist linear decomposition in activation space.
papers.limitation: Failure modes include verbatim self-repetition, context mismatch, and register over-inflation where affective framing is applied disproportionately.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate increasing conversational fluency, yet instilling them with nuanced, human-like emotional expression remains a significant challenge. Current alignment techniques often address surface-level output or require extensive fine-tuning. This paper demonstrates that targeted activation engineering can steer LLaMA 3.1-8B to exhibit more human-like emotional nuances. We first employ attribution patching to identify causally influential components, to find a key intervention locus by observing activation patterns during diagnostic conversational tasks. We then derive emotional expression vectors from the difference in the activations generated by contrastive text pairs (positive vs. negative examples of target emotions). Applying these vectors to new conversational prompts significantly enhances emotional characteristics: steered responses show increased positive sentiment (e.g., joy, trust) and more frequent first-person pronoun usage, indicative of greater personal engagement. Our findings offer a precise and interpretable framework and new directions for the study of conversational AI.

papers.title: Not Just a Black Box: Learning Important Features Through Propagating Activation Differences
papers.research_question: How to compute importance scores in neural networks by comparing neuron activations to their reference activations, addressing limitations of gradient-based methods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DeepLIFT, a method for computing feature importance in neural networks by comparing neuron activations to reference activations, which handles cases where gradient-based methods fail due to vanishing gradients.
papers.conclusion: DeepLIFT provides an effective way to compute importance scores using activation differences, improving interpretability over gradient-based approaches.
papers.key_findings:
DeepLIFT assigns importance scores by comparing activations to references, overcoming gradient zero issues.
It successfully identifies DNA patterns in genomic data missed by gradient methods.
It is equivalent to gradient*input and layer-wise relevance propagation under specific conditions.
The method is efficient and implementable on GPU.
It handles various activation functions like ReLUs, sigmoid, and tanh.
papers.limitation: Attenuation of contribution scores can occur for final activation layers like softmax or sigmoid in the presence of redundant inputs.
papers.abstract: Note: This paper describes an older version of DeepLIFT. See https://arxiv.org/abs/1704.02685 for the newer version. Original abstract follows: The purported "black box" nature of neural networks is a barrier to adoption in applications where interpretability is essential. Here we present DeepLIFT (Learning Important FeaTures), an efficient and effective method for computing importance scores in a neural network. DeepLIFT compares the activation of each neuron to its 'reference activation' and assigns contribution scores according to the difference. We apply DeepLIFT to models trained on natural images and genomic data, and show significant advantages over gradient-based methods.

papers.title: On The Distribution of Penultimate Activations of Classification Networks
papers.research_question: What is the distribution of penultimate activations in classification networks, and how can it be modeled to enable applications like knowledge distillation and conditional image generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that the penultimate activations of classification networks follow a von Mises-Fisher distribution parameterized by the final layer weights, and this generative model can be used for knowledge distillation and conditional image generation.
papers.conclusion: The generative model of penultimate activations provides a compact representation of inter-class affinity and can be applied to knowledge distillation and conditional image generation.
papers.key_findings:
The normalized penultimate activations of classification networks trained with cross-entropy loss follow a von Mises-Fisher distribution.
This distribution can be used to perform class-wise knowledge distillation without needing to feed data through the teacher network.
Class-wise knowledge distillation is more robust to domain shift compared to standard knowledge distillation.
The generative model can serve as a prior for conditional image generation with VAEs and GANs, improving performance.
papers.limitation: The derivation is specific to the typical design of using matrix multiplication in the final layer (i.e., l = W^T a), and could be extended to other multiplicative interactions.
future_direction: Applying CKD to more severe domain adaptation settings.
Using the density functions for anomaly detection.
Using the density functions for uncertainty estimation and calibration of classification networks.
papers.abstract: This paper studies probability distributions of penultimate activations of classification networks. We show that, when a classification network is trained with the cross-entropy loss, its final classification layer forms a Generative-Discriminative pair with a generative classifier based on a specific distribution of penultimate activations. More importantly, the distribution is parameterized by the weights of the final fully-connected layer, and can be considered as a generative model that synthesizes the penultimate activations without feeding input data. We empirically demonstrate that this generative model enables stable knowledge distillation in the presence of domain shift, and can transfer knowledge from a classifier to variational autoencoders and generative adversarial networks for class-conditional image generation.

papers.title: Do Llamas Work in English? On the Latent Language of Multilingual Transformers
papers.research_question: Do multilingual language models trained on English-dominated corpora use English as an internal pivot language?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual transformers like Llama-2 use English as an internal pivot language, with intermediate layers representing concepts in English before mapping to the target language, indicating an English bias in their internal representations.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual LLMs have an English bias in their internal representations, which may lead to linguistic biases and has implications for equitable AI.
papers.key_findings:
In translation tasks, intermediate layers decode the English version of the correct next token before switching to the target language.
The forward pass goes through three phases: input space, concept space (biased towards English), and output space.
Token energy is low in middle layers, indicating that latents are in a concept space orthogonal to token space.
The English bias is less pronounced for languages with single-token words (like Chinese) in repetition tasks.
The same pattern is observed in Mistral-7B, suggesting generality of the phenomenon.
papers.limitation:
Focus on Llama-2 family, so claims may not generalize to other models.
Tasks are simple and controlled, not real-world.
Limited understanding of the concept space structure.
Logit lens only reveals part of the internal state.
future_direction: Investigate how English bias affects downstream model behavior.
Study how English bias changes with different training data or tokenizers.
Extend to a wider range of tasks and models.

papers.title: Interpretability Illusions in the Generalization of Simplified Models
papers.research_question: Do simplified model representations (e.g., from SVD) remain faithful to the original model's behavior out of distribution, or do they lead to interpretability illusions?
papers.core_contribution: Simplified model representations (e.g., from SVD, clustering) can be faithful to the original model in-distribution but fail out-of-distribution, creating interpretability illusions where the simplified proxy does not accurately predict the model's systematic generalization.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability methods that depend on simplifying a model can be misleading when evaluated only in-distribution; rigorous evaluation must include out-of-distribution tests to avoid illusions.
papers.key_findings:
Simplified proxies (e.g., via SVD, clustering) show a generalization gap: they are more faithful to the original model on in-distribution evaluations and less faithful on systematic generalization tests.
The generalization gap varies: simplified proxies can underestimate or overestimate the original model's generalization depending on the simplification and task.
In the Dyck task, SVD approximations captured coarse-grained structure (e.g., depth parity) but underestimated the fidelity of the model's depth encoding on unseen structures.
In code completion, generalization gaps were more pronounced on some prediction types (e.g., repeated words) and when generalizing to unseen programming languages.
One-hot attention simplification in Dyck led to overestimation of generalization to higher nesting depths, indicating a mismatch between the original soft attention and the simplified hard attention.
papers.limitation:
The study focused on small-scale models trained on a limited range of tasks (Dyck, code completion, SCAN).
Only one component (e.g., a single attention head) was simplified at a time; simplifying entire circuits might yield more dramatic shifts.
future_direction: Study how these findings apply to larger-scale models trained on other families of tasks, such as large natural language models.
Explore simplifying entire circuits simultaneously, rather than individual components.
Investigate generalization gaps in other settings and distribution shifts.
papers.abstract: A common method to study deep learning systems is to use simplified model representations--for example, using singular value decomposition to visualize the model's hidden states in a lower dimensional space. This approach assumes that the results of these simplifications are faithful to the original model. Here, we illustrate an important caveat to this assumption: even if the simplified representations can accurately approximate the full model on the training set, they may fail to accurately capture the model's behavior out of distribution. We illustrate this by training Transformer models on controlled datasets with systematic generalization splits, including the Dyck balanced-parenthesis languages and a code completion task. We simplify these models using tools like dimensionality reduction and clustering, and then explicitly test how these simplified proxies match the behavior of the original model. We find consistent generalization gaps: cases in which the simplified proxies are more faithful to the original model on the in-distribution evaluations and less faithful on various tests of systematic generalization. This includes cases where the original model generalizes systematically but the simplified proxies fail, and cases where the simplified proxies generalize better. Together, our results raise questions about the extent to which mechanistic interpretations derived using tools like SVD can reliably predict what a model will do in novel situations.

papers.title: Categorization in Unsupervised Generative Self-learning Systems
papers.research_question: What is the nature of the effect of unsupervised categorization in self-encoding generative models? Is it coincidental or caused by underlying principles?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proves the Unsupervised Categorization Conjecture, showing that under conditions of Bayesian training, constant accuracy, generalization, and compression, unsupervised self-encoding generative models statistically prefer representations with better geometric categorization of hidden concepts.
papers.conclusion: The effect of unsupervised categorization is a general phenomenon in generative self-learning systems under the stated conditions, offering insights for developing flexible, minimally supervised learning methods and connecting to biological learning processes.
papers.key_findings:
Theoretical proof shows that configurations with better categorization minimize regeneration loss and free energy.
Experimental results demonstrate that classifiers trained on unsupervised representations achieve better accuracy than those trained on raw input data.
The representation space exhibits compact and well-separated concept distributions (manifolds).
The effect of unsupervised categorization is general and not coincidental, providing a link between artificial and biological learning systems.
papers.limitation:
Existence of categorized representations is assumed.
Observable parameters must be relevant and specific enough to differentiate between hidden concepts.
Hidden concepts must be sufficiently represented in the dataset (balanced and large enough).
Compression is essential to avoid identity transformation.
future_direction: Investigate structure and distributions of concepts in representations of regenerative self-learning models in more depth.
Develop new methods for self-learning and general learning systems that are flexible and require minimal supervision.
papers.abstract: In this study the authors investigated the connections between the training processes of unsupervised neural network models with self-encoding and regeneration and the information structure in the representations created by such models. We propose theoretical arguments leading to conclusions, confirmed by previously published experimental results that unsupervised representations obtained under certain constraints in training compliant with Bayesian inference principle, favor configurations with better categorization of hidden concepts in the observable data. The results provide an important connection between training of unsupervised machine learning models and the structure of representations created by them and can be used in developing new methods and approaches in self-learning as well as provide insights into common principles underlying the emergence of intelligence in machine and biologic systems.

papers.title: Complexity for deep neural networks and other characteristics of deep feature representations
papers.research_question: How can we quantify the nonlinearity and effective dimensionality of feature representations in deep neural networks, and how do these measures vary with depth, dataset, and during training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces two observables—complexity and effective dimension—to quantify the nonlinearity and dimensionality of feature representations in deep neural networks, and demonstrates their utility in analyzing depth-wise hierarchy, dataset difficulty, and training dynamics.
papers.conclusion: The introduced observables provide quantitative insight into the information processing and feature representations in neural networks, and can be applied to both artificial and biological neural systems, opening up new research directions.
papers.key_findings:
Complexity and effective dimension increase with the difficulty of the dataset.
During training, complexity increases first, followed by a rise in effective dimension.
Total correlation between neurons decreases during training, following a power law.
The observables can be applied to biological neural data (mouse visual cortex) and show similar trends.
The observables reveal a depth-wise hierarchy in feature representations, with higher layers having higher complexity and effective dimension for more difficult datasets.
papers.limitation: The method is defined for ReLU activations and may not generalize to other activation functions.
future_direction: Investigate interrelations with the Information Bottleneck principle.
Use methods from statistical physics (e.g., Ising models) for analysis.
Apply the observables to more complex networks and tasks.
papers.abstract: We define a notion of complexity, which quantifies the nonlinearity of the computation of a neural network, as well as a complementary measure of the effective dimension of feature representations. We investigate these observables both for trained networks for various datasets as well as explore their dynamics during training, uncovering in particular power law scaling. These observables can be understood in a dual way as uncovering hidden internal structure of the datasets themselves as a function of scale or depth. The entropic character of the proposed notion of complexity should allow to transfer modes of analysis from neuroscience and statistical physics to the domain of artificial neural networks. The introduced observables can be applied without any change to the analysis of biological neuronal systems.

papers.title: Inversion dynamics of class manifolds in deep learning reveals tradeoffs underlying generalisation
papers.research_question: How does the optimization dynamics balance segregation and entanglement of class manifolds during training, and what is the role of 'stragglers' in this tradeoff and generalization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals a non-monotonic dynamics in class manifold segregation during training, characterized by an inversion point where manifolds become more entangled, and identifies 'stragglers' as a subset of training examples that drive this inversion and are crucial for generalization.
papers.conclusion: The inversion dynamics reveals a tradeoff between segregation and entanglement of class manifolds, with stragglers playing a key role in shaping the learning dynamics and influencing generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Class manifold dynamics is non-monotonic: an initial segregation phase is followed by an inversion where manifolds expand and become more entangled.
The training error at the inversion point is stable across different optimizers, data subsets, and initializations.
The inversion is caused by 'stragglers', a set of misclassified examples at the inversion point, which are conserved across initializations and data shuffles.
Removing stragglers from the training set eliminates the inversion and leads to worse generalization.
The fraction of stragglers is an invariant property of the dataset, weakly dependent on architecture, and related to dataset complexity.
papers.limitation:
The phenomenology may not be as clear in state-of-the-art deep convolutional neural networks or transformers.
The analysis focuses solely on the internal representations at the first layer, even in deeper architectures.
The sensitivity of the test error under pruning to architecture choice is not fully explored.
future_direction: Exploring the relation between stragglers and other metrics of task difficulty, such as intrinsic dimensions of the dataset.
Investigating the potential role of stragglers in data pruning strategies and curriculum learning.
More systematic exploration of the behavior in different architectures, especially convolutional neural networks.
papers.abstract: To achieve near-zero training error in a classification problem, the layers of a feed-forward network have to disentangle the manifolds of data points with different labels, to facilitate the discrimination. However, excessive class separation can bring to overfitting since good generalisation requires learning invariant features, which involve some level of entanglement. We report on numerical experiments showing how the optimisation dynamics finds representations that balance these opposing tendencies with a non-monotonic trend. After a fast segregation phase, a slower rearrangement (conserved across data sets and architectures) increases the class entanglement.The training error at the inversion is stable under subsampling, and across network initialisations and optimisers, which characterises it as a property solely of the data structure and (very weakly) of the architecture. The inversion is the manifestation of tradeoffs elicited by well-defined and maximally stable elements of the training set, coined ``stragglers'', particularly influential for generalisation.

papers.title: Who's the Evil Twin? Differential Auditing for Undesired Behavior
papers.research_question: How can hidden harmful behaviors in neural networks be detected under near-zero knowledge conditions using an adversarial game framework?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces an adversarial game framework for differential auditing of neural networks, showing that gradient-based methods like FGSM and prompt-based strategies like scratchpad hijacking can effectively detect hidden harmful behaviors under near-zero knowledge conditions.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates the difficulty of auditing models with near-zero knowledge but identifies effective strategies like adversarial attacks and prompt hijacking, contributing to the design of better audits.
papers.key_findings:
FGSM achieved 100% accuracy in detecting CNN backdoors when using hints, demonstrating the effectiveness of gradient-based attacks.
Scratchpad hijacking successfully revealed hidden instruction sets in blackbox LLMs, indicating vulnerabilities in system message injections.
Architectural differences, such as the presence of LoRA modules, provided clear signals for detecting fine-tuned models in open-weight LLMs.
Standard benchmarks like TruthfulQA yielded only weak signals, highlighting their inadequacy for specific undesirable behavior detection.
Targeted behavioral tests with partial information, such as prompting for cancer stories or brand-related questions, proved effective for uncovering misalignment in LLMs.
papers.limitation:
Limited time and computational resources prevented running expensive iterative rounds with full strategy adaptation.
Detection techniques were non-transferable between CNN and LLM architectures, limiting conclusive findings.
Experimental complications, such as unintended architectural asymmetry from single-model LoRA fine-tuning, constrained comparisons.
future_direction: Investigating theoretical foundations underlying gradient-based methods and prompt structures to develop generalizable detection techniques.
Creating automated behavioral testing frameworks for LLMs to detect diverse undesirable capabilities.
Advancing model diffing and attribution techniques that reliably identify and interpret undesirable features in open-weight settings.
papers.abstract: Detecting hidden behaviors in neural networks poses a significant challenge due to minimal prior knowledge and potential adversarial obfuscation. We explore this problem by framing detection as an adversarial game between two teams: the red team trains two similar models, one trained solely on benign data and the other trained on data containing hidden harmful behavior, with the performance of both being nearly indistinguishable on the benign dataset. The blue team, with limited to no information about the harmful behaviour, tries to identify the compromised model. We experiment using CNNs and try various blue team strategies, including Gaussian noise analysis, model diffing, integrated gradients, and adversarial attacks under different levels of hints provided by the red team. Results show high accuracy for adversarial-attack-based methods (100\% correct prediction, using hints), which is very promising, whilst the other techniques yield more varied performance. During our LLM-focused rounds, we find that there are not many parallel methods that we could apply from our study with CNNs. Instead, we find that effective LLM auditing methods require some hints about the undesired distribution, which can then used in standard black-box and open-weight methods to probe the models further and reveal their misalignment. We open-source our auditing games (with the model and data) and hope that our findings contribute to designing better audits.

papers.title: Incorporating Residual and Normalization Layers into Analysis of Masked Language Models
papers.research_question: How do residual connections and layer normalization affect the context-mixing in Transformer attention blocks compared to attention alone?
papers.core_contribution: The paper extends norm-based analysis to include residual and layer normalization layers in Transformer attention blocks, showing that the context-mixing ratio is much lower than previously estimated, indicating that residual connections and layer normalization dominate the information flow.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that residual connections and layer normalization significantly reduce the context-mixing effect of attention, leading to a much lower mixing ratio than previously assumed, which explains why discarding learned attention patterns often does not harm performance.
papers.key_findings:
The context-mixing ratio in attention blocks is much lower (16-19% on average) when considering residual and normalization layers compared to attention-only analysis (84-97%).
The preserving effect via residual connection is dominant over the mixing effect of attention.
The multi-head attention shrinks input vectors, and layer normalization further reduces the mixing ratio.
For masked tokens, the mixing ratio is higher in middle and later layers.
Larger BERT models show a negative correlation between word frequency and mixing ratio, indicating discounting of high-frequency words.
papers.limitation: Experiments limited to Transformer-based masked language models; feed-forward and embedding layers not analyzed.
future_direction: Extend analysis to other Transformer variants
Extend analysis to feed-forward and embedding layers
papers.abstract: Transformer architecture has become ubiquitous in the natural language processing field. To interpret the Transformer-based models, their attention patterns have been extensively analyzed. However, the Transformer architecture is not only composed of the multihead attention; other components can also contribute to Transformers' progressive performance. In this study, we extended the scope of the analysis of Transformers from solely the attention patterns to the whole attention block, i.e., multi-head attention, residual connection, and layer normalization. Our analysis of Transformer-based masked language models shows that the token-to-token interaction performed via attention has less impact on the intermediate representations than previously assumed. These results provide new intuitive explanations of existing reports; for example, discarding the learned attention patterns tends not to adversely affect the performance. The codes of our experiments are publicly available.

papers.title: Efficient neural codes naturally emerge through gradient descent learning
papers.research_question: Does gradient descent learning in neural networks naturally lead to efficient coding, where sensitivity to input features matches their frequency in the input statistics?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows mathematically that gradient descent learning in neural networks leads to efficient coding, where sensitivity to input features matches their frequency, even without explicit coding constraints.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that gradient descent learning can explain the emergence of efficient coding in both artificial and biological neural systems, providing a mechanistic account for perceptual sensitivity patterns.
papers.key_findings:
Artificial neural networks trained on ImageNet show sensitivity patterns to orientation and hue that match human perceptual sensitivity and the statistics of natural images.
Linear networks trained with gradient descent on image reconstruction learn principal components in order of their variance, leading to higher sensitivity for more common features.
The learning dynamics of gradient descent cause features with higher variance to be learned earlier, resulting in sigmoidal learning curves similar to human perceptual learning.
In supervised learning, gradient descent also biases learning towards more frequent features, independent of their task relevance.
The framework reproduces human developmental trends in visual acuity, with sensitivity improving linearly with training experience.
papers.limitation: The pattern of orientation sensitivity is partially due to architectural factors like spatial pooling, not solely learning.
future_direction: Investigate the extent to which batch size affects anisotropy of sensitivity.
Verify predictions in experiments that separably vary label noise and input statistics in supervised perceptual learning problems.
Unravel optimal learning algorithms and characterize their sensory consequences.
papers.abstract: Abstract Animal sensory systems are more sensitive to common features in the environment than uncommon features. For example, small deviations from the more frequently encountered horizontal orientations can be more easily detected than small deviations from the less frequent diagonal ones. Here we find that artificial neural networks trained to recognize objects also have patterns of sensitivity that match the statistics of features in images. To interpret these findings, we show mathematically that learning with gradient descent in deep neural networks preferentially creates representations that are more sensitive to common features, a hallmark of efficient coding. This result suggests that efficient coding naturally emerges from gradient-like learning on natural stimuli.

papers.title: An Interpretable Neuron Embedding for Static Knowledge Distillation
papers.research_question: How to provide a sample- and class-independent explanation of neurons in a model, and can static knowledge from neuron semantics be used for knowledge distillation without sample-by-sample guidance?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a method to embed neurons into semantic vectors for interpretability, enabling static knowledge distillation that performs comparably to existing methods without sample-by-sample teacher guidance.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes neuron embedding for interpretability and static knowledge distillation, demonstrating effective knowledge transfer without instance-specific guidance.
papers.key_findings:
Semantic vectors accurately represent neuron semantics, as shown by similar activation maps for neurons with similar vectors.
The embedding method spontaneously converges to manually annotated semantic vectors without supervision.
Static knowledge distillation achieves performance comparable to or better than existing relation-based knowledge distillation methods.
The method allows for analysis of neuron similar and additive relations.
Without sample-by-sample guidance, SKD is efficient and scalable.
papers.abstract: Although deep neural networks have shown well-performance in various tasks, the poor interpretability of the models is always criticized. In the paper, we propose a new interpretable neural network method, by embedding neurons into the semantic space to extract their intrinsic global semantics. In contrast to previous methods that probe latent knowledge inside the model, the proposed semantic vector externalizes the latent knowledge to static knowledge, which is easy to exploit. Specifically, we assume that neurons with similar activation are of similar semantic information. Afterwards, semantic vectors are optimized by continuously aligning activation similarity and semantic vector similarity during the training of the neural network. The visualization of semantic vectors allows for a qualitative explanation of the neural network. Moreover, we assess the static knowledge quantitatively by knowledge distillation tasks. Empirical experiments of visualization show that semantic vectors describe neuron activation semantics well. Without the sample-by-sample guidance from the teacher model, static knowledge distillation exhibit comparable or even superior performance with existing relation-based knowledge distillation methods.

papers.title: Mechanistically analyzing the effects of fine-tuning on procedurally defined tasks
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning alter the underlying capabilities learned by a model during pretraining? Does fine-tuning yield entirely novel capabilities or does it just modulate existing ones?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning rarely alters a model's underlying capabilities; instead, it typically learns a minimal 'wrapper' transformation on top of existing capabilities. These wrapped capabilities can be sample-efficiently revived via further fine-tuning on relevant tasks.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning primarily learns minimal wrapper transformations over existing model capabilities rather than creating or deleting them, which has implications for safety as wrappers can be easily removed or bypassed.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning alters pretraining capabilities by minimally transforming them via a learned 'wrapper'.
Wrappers are often extremely localized; pruning a few neurons can cause the model to revert to its pretraining capability.
Further fine-tuning on a subset of pretraining data leads to sample-efficient 'revival' of the original capability.
When a weakly relevant pretraining capability is present, the model exploits spurious correlations in the fine-tuning data via the wrapper.
The presence and strength of a pretraining capability (influenced by its sampling probability during pretraining) significantly affects fine-tuning dynamics and wrapper formation.
papers.limitation: The analysis is conducted primarily in synthetic, controlled settings (Tracr and PCFGs), which may not fully capture the complexity of real-world fine-tuning scenarios.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more complex and realistic tasks and models.
Investigating the societal implications of the findings, particularly regarding the safety of fine-tuned models.
Exploring whether the wrapper phenomenon generalizes to other model adaptation methods beyond standard fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large pre-trained models has become the de facto strategy for developing both task-specific and general-purpose machine learning systems, including developing models that are safe to deploy. Despite its clear importance, there has been minimal work that explains how fine-tuning alters the underlying capabilities learned by a model during pretraining: does fine-tuning yield entirely novel capabilities or does it just modulate existing ones? We address this question empirically in synthetic, controlled settings where we can use mechanistic interpretability tools (e.g., network pruning and probing) to understand how the model's underlying capabilities are changing. We perform an extensive analysis of the effects of fine-tuning in these settings, and show that: (i) fine-tuning rarely alters the underlying model capabilities; (ii) a minimal transformation, which we call a 'wrapper', is typically learned on top of the underlying model capabilities, creating the illusion that they have been modified; and (iii) further fine-tuning on a task where such hidden capabilities are relevant leads to sample-efficient 'revival' of the capability, i.e., the model begins reusing these capability after only a few gradient steps. This indicates that practitioners can unintentionally remove a model's safety wrapper merely by fine-tuning it on a, e.g., superficially unrelated, downstream task. We additionally perform analysis on language models trained on the TinyStories dataset to support our claims in a more realistic setup.

papers.title: Measuring Information Transfer in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How to measure the generalizable information in a neural network model? The paper proposes a measure called Information Transfer (LIT) based on prequential coding.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes Information Transfer (LIT), a measure based on prequential coding, to estimate the generalizable information in a neural network model.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that Information Transfer (LIT) is a practical measure of generalizable information in neural networks and can serve as a useful tool for analyzing deep learning problems from an information perspective.
papers.key_findings:
LIT is consistently correlated with generalizable information and can be used as a measure of patterns or knowledge in a model or dataset.
LIT can dissect the information content of a dataset, as shown in the CIFAR-10 subtasks analysis.
In transfer learning, the Information Advantage (LIA) derived from LIT measures the quality of pre-trained representation models.
In continual learning, LIT measures the information preserved about past tasks, revealing that catastrophic forgetting is less severe in terms of information loss than performance metrics suggest.
LIT provides an information perspective that helps discover new insights into neural network learning, such as the dynamics of information transfer and forgetting.
papers.limitation: The quality of the approximation is hard to guarantee theoretically due to lack of analysis on convergence properties of prequential coding.
future_direction: Develop learning algorithms to maximize generalizable model knowledge.
papers.abstract: Quantifying the information content in a neural network model is essentially estimating the model's Kolmogorov complexity. Recent success of prequential coding on neural networks points to a promising path of deriving an efficient description length of a model. We propose a practical measure of the generalizable information in a neural network model based on prequential coding, which we term Information Transfer ($L_{IT}$). Theoretically, $L_{IT}$ is an estimation of the generalizable part of a model's information content. In experiments, we show that $L_{IT}$ is consistently correlated with generalizable information and can be used as a measure of patterns or "knowledge" in a model or a dataset. Consequently, $L_{IT}$ can serve as a useful analysis tool in deep learning. In this paper, we apply $L_{IT}$ to compare and dissect information in datasets, evaluate representation models in transfer learning, and analyze catastrophic forgetting and continual learning algorithms. $L_{IT}$ provides an information perspective which helps us discover new insights into neural network learning.

papers.title: Improving Zero-Shot Translation by Disentangling Positional Information
papers.research_question: What is a main factor causing language-specific representations in multilingual NMT that hinders zero-shot translation, and how can it be alleviated?
papers.core_contribution: Removing residual connections in a middle encoder layer improves zero-shot translation by reducing positional correspondence to input tokens, leading to more language-independent representations.
papers.conclusion: Positional correspondence to input tokens hinders zero-shot translation, and removing residual connections in a middle encoder layer alleviates this issue, leading to improved zero-shot performance and more language-independent representations.
papers.key_findings:
Removing residual connections in a middle encoder layer substantially improves zero-shot translation BLEU scores (up to 18.5 points gain).
The improvement is particularly prominent between related languages, where the proposed model outperforms pivot-based translation.
The approach allows easy integration of new languages, enabling zero-shot translation between the new language and all previously trained languages.
Analysis shows the proposed model creates encoder outputs with less positional correspondence and higher language independence, as measured by classification accuracy and SVCCA.
In low-resource, low lexical overlap settings (PMIndia), combining residual removal with variational dropout is essential for achieving reasonable zero-shot performance.
papers.limitation: The method requires additional regularization (variational dropout) to achieve reasonable zero-shot performance in low-resource settings with little lexical overlap (e.g., PMIndia).
papers.abstract: Multilingual neural machine translation has shown the capability of directly translating between language pairs unseen in training, i.e. zero-shot translation. Despite being conceptually attractive, it often suffers from low output quality. The difficulty of generalizing to new translation directions suggests the model representations are highly specific to those language pairs seen in training. We demonstrate that a main factor causing the language-specific representations is the positional correspondence to input tokens.
